summary: A perennial evergreen native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, it forms a crown of rigid, bayonet-like leaves above a conspicuous trunk. Native Americans ate its flowers and fruit raw or roasted and ground its black seeds into flour.
edibilityNote: Native Americans ate the flowers and fruit raw or roasted and ground the black seeds into flour.

summary: Grass native to temperate Europe, although its precise native range is unknown. Depending on conditions, it may be annual, biennial, or perennial; it has a round stem and spikelets tipped with a long bristle.

A herbaceous perennial native across temperate and Arctic regions of Europe, northwest Africa, Asia and the Americas, sea plantain forms a dense rosette of thick, fleshy leaves. Its leaves and seeds are eaten raw or cooked, and the seeds can be ground into flour.
edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; the seeds can also be ground into flour.

summary: An annual flowering herb native to the Americas, garden cosmos has finely divided, threadlike foliage and conspicuous flower heads with pink, violet or white outer petals surrounding yellow centres. It is widely grown as an ornamental and may return by self-sowing.

A filamentous terrestrial green alga, Trentepohlia aurea has no native origin specified in the supplied information. It forms small, bushy tufts ranging from golden yellow to orange-brown and grows on surfaces including rocks, old walls, tree bark, rotting wood, mosses and wet soil.

A deciduous tree native to tropical and southern Asia. Its hard, smooth fruit has six vertical furrows and a sour, bitter, astringent taste; it is eaten raw or cooked and is often pickled in South Asia.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw or cooked and used in South Asian pickles, savoury dishes and candied sweets.

summary: Flowering tree native to the Indian subcontinent and adjacent parts of Southeast Asia. It bears abundant hanging clusters of yellow flowers and long, pungent-smelling seed pods. In India, people sometimes eat the flowers.
edibilityNote: In India, the flowers are sometimes eaten by people.

summary: A fast-growing deciduous or semi-deciduous tree native from Assam and southern China through Malesia and Papuasia to Queensland. Its open clusters of pale-pink to crimson flowers have yellow stamens, while its fruit develops in long, cylindrical dark-brown pods.

Cherry tree thought to have originated on the Iranian Plateau or in Eastern Europe, although truly wild populations may no longer exist. Its acidic fruit has edible sour pulp, with dark-red Morello and lighter-red Amarelle as its two main cultivar groups.
edibilityNote: The sour fruit pulp is edible; dried cherries are cooked in savoury dishes and desserts or made into fruit spreads.

summary: An annual, downy herb found in southern Europe, southwestern Asia, North Africa and Macaronesia. It bears rounded or egg-shaped clusters of pink flowers and grows chiefly in sandy, temporarily flooded grassland depressions, sometimes on slightly salty or loamy soil.

Annual mercury is an annual herb native to the Middle East and Mediterranean region. Its branched, ridged stems release watery sap when broken, and its nearly hairless leaves grow in opposite pairs. Plants may be male, female or hermaphrodite, an unusually varied breeding system.
edibilityNote: It is not known whether annual mercury is poisonous to humans; documented poisonings concern the related dog's mercury.

summary: A bulb-forming perennial native to parts of Europe, North Africa and Asia. Its dense spikes carry dark blue flowers with white tips, sometimes topped by a cluster of paler, sterile flowers.

An annual flowering plant native to Europe, southwestern Asia, North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Korea and Japan. It has a sprawling habit, usually bold blue flowers and dull green, toothed leaves; its hairy fruit capsule has two parallel lobes.

Perennial flowering herb native to Europe. It resembles a small strawberry plant but produces no fleshy fruit; its matte, dark-green leaflets usually have a shorter central tooth than the adjacent teeth.

An evergreen perennial native to the eastern and central United States. It forms low mats of hairy, narrow leaves, covered in late spring and early summer by small flowers in shades including pink, white, blue and mauve.

A small herbaceous perennial endemic to South Africa’s western Cape region. It has grass-like leaves and spring flowers that are pink with yellow throats; outside its native range, it has naturalised widely and is considered an environmental weed in much of Australia.

Chilli pepper native to the Americas, with a possible centre of origin in the tropical northern Amazon. Its varieties have distinctive flavours and range from non-spicy to exceptionally hot. Fruits vary greatly in shape and colour, commonly ripening red, orange or yellow.
edibilityNote: Used for millennia in Yucatán and Caribbean cooking, especially in stews, sauces and marinades for meat and chicken.

summary: An endangered, fast-growing deciduous conifer whose remaining wild populations are confined to south-central China. Its bright-green opposite leaves turn reddish brown in autumn, and it can grow into a very tall tree despite being the shortest redwood.

An annual or short-lived perennial native to Florida, Mexico, the West Indies and tropical Central and South America, it grows low with translucent, succulent-like branching stems. Its tiny leaves occur in unequal pairs, and the male flowers explosively eject pollen.

An evergreen vine native to Mo'orea in French Polynesia. It climbs with aerial roots, and its heart-shaped juvenile leaves become irregularly divided when mature. It rarely flowers without artificial hormone treatment.
edibilityNote: Consumption may cause burning or swelling around the mouth and other reactions because the plant contains calcium oxalate.

summary: A perennial ornamental herb whose native range is unclear, Buddha’s hand taro is known only from cultivation and plants near homes or in disturbed places. It has broad, roughly heart-shaped leaves and rarely produces flowers or red berries.
edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous when eaten because it contains calcium oxalate crystals.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to Ecuador and southwestern Colombia, painter's-palette has a brightly coloured red or pink leaf surrounding a projecting white or yellow flower spike. It flowers throughout the year, and the whole plant is toxic if eaten.
edibilityNote: The whole plant is toxic; ingestion can cause mouth and throat irritation, salivation, difficulty swallowing and vomiting.

summary: Small creeping flowering plant native to Europe. It has square stems, opposite blunt-toothed leaves and tiny flowers surrounded by bright yellow-green leafy bracts, typically in damp, shady woodland or beside streams.

A small herb native to the British Isles, Europe, North Africa, Turkey and Iran, it may be annual, biennial or a short-lived perennial. It has mostly basal leaves with rounded leaflets, tiny white flowers and fruits that generally remain below the flowers.
edibilityNote: In Manipur it is reportedly eaten as an aromatic herb and eromba garnish, but the source marks this claim as needing a citation.

summary: A tufted sedge native across Europe and into parts of Asia as far east as Iran. Its flowering stems carry several dangling female spikes beneath one slender male spike, and it typically grows in deciduous woodland on heavy soils.

summary: A dewberry native to the central and eastern United States, eastern Canada and northern Mexico. It grows as a low shrub or woody vine with prickly stems whose young tips sometimes root into the ground; its ripe dark-purple berries have a tart-sweet flavour.
edibilityNote: Ripe berries are eaten raw or used in preserves, pies and cobblers.

summary: Coniferous tree native to the Atlantic coast of North America, where it grows almost exclusively in freshwater wetlands. It has feathery green to blue-green foliage and mature bark with deep ridges.

A large conifer native to the Himalayas, from eastern Afghanistan to southwestern Tibet, western Nepal, northern Pakistan and north-central India. It has a cone-shaped crown, level branches and drooping branchlets, with needles growing singly or in dense clusters.

A semi-evergreen oak native to the southeastern coastal plains and south-central United States. Its broad, mostly unlobed leaves have bristle tips and fall as new growth begins, while its acorns ripen blackish-brown about 18 months after pollination.

A flowering plant native to the Caribbean and south Florida, pineland croton grows in pine rocklands, marl prairies, coastal strands and disturbed uplands. It is considered threatened in south Florida because much of its habitat has been lost to development.

An erect annual herb native to Europe. Its slender stem is covered in hairs and sticky glands, while its magenta tubular flowers may have white areas and bear two raised yellow structures in the throat.

A clump-forming, round-stemmed perennial rush native to North America, slender path rush has short basal leaves and clusters of small, egg-shaped seed capsules at the tops of its stems. The capsules split into three parts when ripe, and the plant also spreads through underground roots.

A perennial grass native to Eurasia and North Africa, and possibly northern North America, creeping bent spreads along the ground to form mats. Its tapering leaves are often blue-grey, and it is widely used as turf, particularly on golf courses.

An annual herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa. Its hairy foliage has narrow leaflets, while its pink flower spikes develop long needle-like lobes that harden into bristles as the plant dries.
Aquatic plant native to Asia and northern Australia. It is endangered in China and Japan amid habitat loss and deterioration, but is an invasive weed in America.

A small tree or shrub native to the tropical Americas, though its exact origin is unknown, sweetsop is widely cultivated in warm regions. Its ripe fruit has a knobbly, segmented rind whose sections tend to separate, revealing fragrant, sweet, custard-like pulp around hard dark seeds. The edible pulp is sold in tropical markets, rarely cooked, and used for juice in Haiti.
edibilityNote: The sweet fruit pulp is edible, usually sold fresh and rarely cooked; in Haiti the fruit is used to make juice.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native to Central and South America, water primrose grows along lakes, ponds, ditches and streams. Its stems may remain underwater or emerge fully, and the plant can form dense mats in still or slow-moving water.

A palm-like evergreen tree of uncertain origin, possibly native to the Mascarene Islands. It has pale-brown prop roots, spiralling leaf scars and stiff leaves edged with red spines. Female plants bear pine-cone-like fruit, which provides a starchy food after cooking.
edibilityNote: The fruit provides a starchy food and is eaten after cooking.

summary: An aromatic, palm-like tree native to Southeast Asia, the Andaman Islands and the Philippines, and also found wild in southern India and Burma. It has spiny, fragrant leaves, brace roots and highly scented flowers used for perfume. Its soft shoots are very astringent and considered inedible unless blanched, after which they taste like bamboo shoots.
edibilityNote: Soft shoots are eaten after blanching; untreated shoots are very astringent and considered inedible.

summary: Small coastal tree native broadly to Malesia, Papuasia, eastern Australia and the Pacific, although extensive cultivation makes its exact native island range uncertain. It is braced by aerial roots and bears large segmented fruit resembling a pineapple. The fruit is edible, but some varieties require thorough cooking, while low-oxalate cultivars can be eaten raw.
edibilityNote: Fruit and slender seeds are eaten; some varieties require thorough cooking because of calcium oxalate, while low-oxalate cultivars may be eaten raw.

summary: A clump-forming perennial herb native to the eastern and central Mediterranean. It has large glossy, lobed leaves and upright spikes of purple and white flowers, and can spread aggressively from seeds and root pieces.

An annual flowering plant native mainly to Mediterranean and sub-Mediterranean regions from southern Europe and North Africa to Western Asia. It has distinctive brick-red flowers, upper leaves ending in simple climbing tendrils, and smooth spherical seeds.

A forest vine endemic to New Zealand. Its large flowers, usually vivid red but sometimes orange or yellow, appear from autumn into spring, while mature rope-like stems hang free after their short clinging roots die.

Forest tree endemic to New Zealand. It often begins life on another tree, later forming a massive, frequently hollow trunk from fused descending roots. Small notched leaves and sprays of dark scarlet flowers are distinctive.

A shrub native to Southern and Eastern Africa, the Azores, the Arabian Peninsula, South Asia and East Asia. Its young leaves are deep red before becoming glossy dark green, while female plants produce small purple berries. Parts are used in milk- and meat-based soups by Batemi and Masai people, and the flowers are eaten.
edibilityNote: Parts are used in milk- and meat-based soups by Batemi and Masai people; the flowers are also eaten.

summary: Annual or perennial herb native to Europe, with hairy stems and sparse, narrow leaves. Its tiny flowers change from yellow or cream to pink and then blue as they mature.
A woody evergreen vine native to Brazil, Costa Rica and Panama. Its large flower has pale pink or whitish veins over a maroon face, a rounded rear and a yellow throat.

Aquatic perennial widespread across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, growing in mud and fresh water. Its lance-shaped leaves become smaller and less prominently veined when submerged. Small pinkish-purple, three-petalled flowers open in the morning from June to August.
A flowering plant whose variety Centranthus calcitrapae var. calcitrapae is native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, but introduced in the Azores.

A flowering plant native to the Mediterranean basin, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Yemen and the Arabian Peninsula. It has lightly woolly, toothed gray-green leaves and long-lasting purple flower spikes topped with pale violet bracts. The whole plant is strongly aromatic.

A biennial herb native to southern Europe and western Asia, it has been cultivated as a leaf vegetable in England since the 17th century. It forms an overwintering rosette before producing bright yellow spring flowers. The leaves are eaten in sandwiches or salads, cooked like spinach, or used in soups and pestos.
edibilityNote: Cultivated in England since the 17th century; leaves are eaten raw in sandwiches or salads, or cooked in several dishes.

summary: A perennial grass native to much of Eurasia, marsh foxtail grows in moist places. It forms bunches of upright stems and dense pale-green to purplish flower clusters with dusty yellow-orange anthers, and can spread by seeds or by rooting at stem joints.
Perennial grass native to Europe and Asia. It forms dense stands on moist, fertile grassland and flowers from April to June, earlier than many similar grasses.

Large evergreen coniferous tree endemic to Japan, sugi has a conical crown and reddish-brown bark that peels in vertical strips. Its blue-green needle-like leaves grow spirally, and its round cones open when dry to release pointed seeds.

A perennial flowering plant native to much of Eurasia and North Africa. Its mostly unbranched stem carries spaced bright pink to magenta flowers, and it is a common weed of cultivated fields and waste places on other continents.

A herbaceous plant with no explicitly stated native origin, found widely in southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia. It has small, bright yellow, buttercup-like flowers and is now restricted to two sites in the British Isles.

A flowering plant found in western and southern Europe, especially around the Mediterranean. This tall wild gladiolus grows up to 50 cm, while Britain’s small New Forest population may have been introduced.
A small perennial herb native to Europe, North Africa and parts of western Asia including Turkey, it has a self-supporting habit and simple, broad leaves.

A perennial herb originating in the northwestern Mediterranean. It has rough, upright stems and purple flower heads surrounded by pale red bracts ending in several spreading or backward-pointing yellowish spines, and commonly occupies dry, disturbed ground, hedges, vineyards and beaches.

A succulent plant native to South Africa, slender iceplant usually grows as an annual, forming low mats of stems. Its small, fleshy cylindrical leaves and green-to-bright-red growth have shiny, bubble-like bumps; wet fruit capsules open to release seeds.

An annual flax native to the Mediterranean region and parts of Africa and Asia. Its rigid stem and light-yellow flowers are distinctive; historically, its green sprouts and tender leaves were cooked in kūtaḥ, while in some cultures roasted, ground flaxseed is eaten with rice.
edibilityNote: Ancient green sprouts and tender leaves were cooked in kūtaḥ; in some cultures, roasted ground flaxseed is eaten with rice, water and salt.

summary: A flowering plant in the daisy family, native to parts of southern Europe and North Africa. It has been introduced elsewhere and grows as a weed in places including California and New South Wales.

A large evergreen conifer native to the Pacific Northwest of North America, it grows in cool, wet forests. Its flattened needles lie beside and above the shoots, leaving their undersides bare, while its dark-purple cones disintegrate when mature.

A dense shrub or small tree native to coastal western and southern Australia, western coastal wattle has golden flower heads and leathery pods containing dark seeds ringed by orange or scarlet tissue. Indigenous Australians grind the seeds into flour for damper, while edible trunk gum is chewed or used to make glue.
edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians grind the seeds into flour for damper; edible gum from the trunk is used as chewing gum.

summary: A flowering tree native to south-eastern Australia and Tasmania, black wattle usually has smooth bark, finely divided leaves and fragrant pale yellow or cream flower heads followed by dark pods. It is considered invasive in some introduced ranges.
edibilityNote: The Ngunnawal people use its gum as food and traditionally cut the bark in autumn to maintain the sap supply.

summary: A large shrub or tree endemic to southeastern South Australia, much of Victoria, eastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland, kangaroo thorn has dense foliage and many long spines. It usually produces small, bright yellow, rounded flower heads between August and November, followed by brown pods containing hard black seeds.
A tree native to southeastern Australia, it has flattened leaf stalks instead of true leaves. Profuse fragrant golden flowers appear from late winter into spring, followed by long seed pods.
edibilityNote: Its gum was eaten by Indigenous Australians and has been investigated as a substitute for gum arabic.

summary: A small tree native to southwestern Western Australia. It has a dense, spreading, weeping form and produces groups of bright-yellow spherical flower heads in late winter and early spring; outside its native range it can become invasive.

A flowering shrub native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, California copperleaf is especially abundant in San Diego County’s hills. Despite its name, its hairy, juicy, toothed leaves are light green rather than copper; its flowers combine a red-and-pink spike with a green cup at the base.
A grass native to the Mediterranean and western Asia, including Palestine and the Levant. Elsewhere it is known as a noxious weed.
Flowering grass species native to continental Portugal.

A succulent subshrub native to the Canary Islands and northern Africa, naturally associated with sandy beaches. Rough woody stems carry rosettes of thick green leaves with red, eyelash-fringed edges, followed by cream-coloured flowers in spring.

An uncommon agave of the United States' desert southwest, Utah agave forms rosettes of sharp, blue-green leaves and can grow in clonal colonies. Its very tall flower cluster bears bulbous yellow or yellow-green flowers. Local Native American peoples, including the Havasupai, historically used the plant for food and fibre.
edibilityNote: The plant was historically used for food and fibre by local Native American peoples, including the Havasupai; no plant part or preparation is specified.

summary: An annual flowering herb of unstated native origin, once a common weed of European wheat fields. Its hairy upright stems bear single deep-pink to purple, scentless flowers, with narrow pointed sepals extending beyond the petals. All parts are poisonous.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; folk medicinal use has carried a risk of fatal poisoning.

summary: Perennial grass native to Eurasia, colonial bent forms dense growth of fine leaves. Its finely branched flowers appear from May to June and resemble a purple haze from a distance, while the seed-bearing branches persist into winter.

An annual grass found across northwestern Africa, western Asia and southern Europe. Its slender stems carry threadlike leaves and an open, loose flower cluster with solitary spikelets; in Crimea it occurs rarely on rocky slopes, woodland clearings and among shrubs.

Small aquatic plant widespread across temperate and subarctic Eurasia, North Africa and parts of North America, with no explicitly stated native origin. Submerged leaves are ribbon-like, while those above water are stiff and broad; underwater flowers remain closed and self-pollinate.

A bulb-forming perennial wild onion native to Europe, northwestern Africa and the Middle East. Every part smells strongly of garlic, and its flower heads commonly contain small bulbils that detach and grow into new plants.
edibilityNote: Leaves, flowers and bulbs are edible, though reports differ on whether they have an unpleasant aftertaste compared with common garlic.

summary: A tree or shrub native to the southern Apennine Mountains and northeastern Corsica. Its glossy green, heart-based leaves have an unusually long season, lasting from April to December in the Northern Hemisphere, while its female catkins mature into hard, woody pseudo-cones.

An aloe native to southern and eastern South Africa, southeastern Botswana and Zimbabwe. Its variable red-to-green leaves always carry distinctive H-shaped spots, while its red-to-yellow flowers form flat-topped clusters. Its seeds are reputedly poisonous.
edibilityNote: The seeds are reputedly poisonous.

summary: Perennial bunchgrass native to much of the temperate Northern Hemisphere, from Eurasia to North America. It usually grows beside fresh water and has cylindrical flower heads whose anthers range from white and yellow to bright orange.

An annual grass native to Eurasia. It often grows in tufts, with hairless leaves and cylindrical flower heads that may be yellow-green, pale green or purple; in the UK it is a major cereal weed with resistance to several herbicides.

Flowering plant native to Central and South America. It has long, ground-hugging stems that often root at lower joints, tiny stiff white flowers, and masses of sharp, detachable V-shaped prickles that can embed in feet and skin.
A herb native to temperate South America that grows both on land and in water. Its sprawling, hollow stems form floating mats, and its small flowers are white and papery.

An annual grey-green herb found in southern Europe, North Africa and the Near East. It is covered with pressed, star-shaped hairs and has yellow flowers followed by rounded, slightly flattened pods; it grows in open disturbed places such as cereal fields, fallow ground, olive groves and eroded slopes.

An annual flowering plant indigenous to the high Peruvian Andes, love-lies-bleeding is known for striking, dense flower clusters that may be black, red or, most commonly, white. Its leaves and seeds are edible; the seeds are eaten as cereal, popped or ground into flour.
edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are edible; seeds are popped, eaten as cereal, or ground into flour for breads, sweets, pasta and noodles.

summary: A short-lived perennial or annual native to South America. It flowers from summer to fall and grows best in weedy or disturbed places.

An annual herb found in North America and Mexico, fringed amaranth has greenish to maroon flowers. In arid regions, it usually blooms after the summer rains and often grows on sandy or gravelly slopes, in semideserts or disturbed habitats.
An annual flowering plant originating as a pioneer species in eastern North America and now introduced widely elsewhere. It is extremely variable, and its seeds and cooked leaves are edible.
edibilityNote: The seeds and cooked leaves are edible; several Native American groups also used the plant as food.

summary: An upright ornamental plant native to Central America and elsewhere in North America. It bears dense summer and autumn flower clusters, usually deep purplish-red, and in Africa and El Salvador its mildly flavored leaves and seeds are valued as food.
edibilityNote: In Africa and El Salvador, the mildly flavored leaves and seeds are valued as food.

summary: An edible flowering plant native to most of the southern half of North America, although eastern United States populations are probably naturalized. It grows rapidly and competes strongly with crops. Native Americans historically ate its seeds and used its cooked or dried greens.
edibilityNote: Leaves, stems and seeds are edible; Native Americans historically ate the seeds and used the plant as a cooked or dried green.

summary: An upright annual herb native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, Powell's amaranth is naturalized across much of the temperate Americas and introduced elsewhere. It bears long, narrow clusters of male and female flowers among spiny green bracts, followed by smooth capsules containing shiny reddish-black seeds.

A summer annual flowering plant native to North America, it is believed to have originally ranged from north of Missouri and Tennessee to the Great Lakes. Its hairless stems and leaves have a bright, glossy appearance, and separate male and female plants bear differently shaped seedheads.

Annual herb native to tropical South America, Central America and the Caribbean. It has a light-green upright stem with many branches from the base. Its leaves are eaten boiled as greens or vegetables, while its nutty seeds are eaten as snacks, used in biscuits or boiled into porridge.
edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten boiled as greens or vegetables; seeds are eaten as snacks, used in biscuits or boiled into porridge.

summary: A herbaceous annual—or biennial that behaves like an annual in cultivation—bullwort is considered indigenous to Egypt or parts of Europe and the Middle East or West Asia; a Nile River Valley origin is hypothesized. It bears white, lace-like flower clusters and contains compounds with strong photosensitizing effects.

Bristly flowering perennial native to Europe, western Asia and the eastern Maghreb. It has lance-shaped leaves and small, tubular, bright violet-blue flowers, which typically appear from May to July and are edible.
edibilityNote: The flowers are edible.

summary: A perennial herb native to northern North America from Alaska to New York and south to Arizona and New Mexico, and also known from parts of South America. Its appearance varies greatly among varieties, with deeply divided hairy leaves and usually white petal-like sepals. It is poisonous and contains high levels of ranunculin in its above-ground parts and roots.
edibilityNote: Poisonous; its above-ground parts and roots contain high levels of ranunculin.

summary: A South American evergreen climbing vine with fleshy, heart-shaped leaves and warty tubers along its stems. The tubers detach easily and spread the plant; its heavy growth can smother vegetation and break branches.
edibilityNote: Leaves and stems are eaten raw or cooked, and rhizomes are edible; the aerial bulbils are inedible.

summary: An annual grass native to North Africa and southern and western Europe. It grows in small tufts, with short, pointed, somewhat hairy leaves and a flat, hairy flower head.

Short-lived perennial grass native to acidic grasslands in Eurasia and northern Africa. It flowers early, in late spring and early summer, and its bright yellow seed heads smell especially strongly when dried, like fresh hay with a hint of vanilla.

Annual or biennial grass native to Eurasia and North Africa, from the Canary Islands through Denmark to Yakutia. It grows in sandy pastures and has become naturalized in the United States, Canada and the Russian Far East.

Aquatic flowering plant native to South Africa’s Western Cape and Mpumalanga provinces. It becomes dormant when seasonal ponds dry, then regrows after autumn rain; its buds and flowers are eaten in waterblommetjiebredie.
edibilityNote: Buds and flowers are eaten in the South African dish waterblommetjiebredie.

summary: A perennial vine native to South America, mainly Peru but also Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay, moth vine produces smelly milky sap that is slightly toxic and may trigger skin allergy. Its scented, cup-shaped flowers can accidentally trap insects by their tongues, sometimes fatally. Large pear-shaped pods contain many black seeds attached to silky hairs.

A biennial plant native to temperate parts of the Old World, from Europe through the Middle East to eastern Asia. Its purple flower heads have hooks that carry mature fruits, while its cultivated root is eaten as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: The root is eaten as a vegetable; peeled tender leaf stalks may be eaten raw or cooked. Roots are also roasted, braised or fermented.

summary: A rosette-forming plant native to Namibia and South Africa’s Cape Provinces, Prostrate Capeweed grows low along the ground. Its creeping runners form a blanket-like cover, with bright yellow daisy-like flowers standing out against pale green, silvery leaves.

An annual or biennial flowering plant whose native origin is not stated, recorded from Nepal to Pakistan and widely distributed in the United Kingdom, southern Poland and China. Ants tend to pollinate it, and its extract is traditionally used for kidney and bladder problems, cough and dysentery.

A herbaceous plant native to the Canary Islands and endemic to Tenerife. It is distinguished by robust stems, crowded blue-green leaves divided two or three times, solitary flower heads and fruits bearing a crown-shaped tuft.

An annual bunchgrass native to the Americas, it is now distributed nearly worldwide. Highly variable with its surroundings, it forms tufts and narrow flower clusters whose fruits each bear three awns.

A perennial herb reported as native either to temperate northern Europe or southwestern Asia. Its pointed tuberous roots are grated as a pungent condiment, while the leaves are also edible; the grated root is often mixed with vinegar and used in sauces.
edibilityNote: The grated root is used as a condiment, often with vinegar; the leaves are also edible.

summary: Tufted grass native throughout Europe, including Iceland, and to western and southwestern Asia and northwestern Africa. It has rough, bright-green leaves and flower clusters that often persist into winter. The bulbous subspecies produces corms at the stem base.

Annual wormwood native to temperate Asia and naturalized in many countries. Its deeply divided leaves have an intense aromatic scent. It is the source of artemisinin used in antimalarial medicine, although the World Health Organization discourages plant infusions for treating malaria.

Aromatic evergreen shrub of the Intermountain West of North America, although the account does not explicitly label this range native. It has pungent silvery foliage with three-lobed leaf tips and can live for more than a century.
edibilityNote: The Cahuilla historically gathered its seeds in quantity and ground them into flour.

summary: A flowering herbaceous perennial found across temperate Europe, Asia and eastern and western North America. It bears feathery plumes of white or cream flowers, with male and female flowers on separate plants. In Italy, young shoots are briefly boiled and then cooked with eggs and cheese or added to a wild-green soup.
edibilityNote: In Italy, young shoots are briefly boiled, then cooked with eggs and cheese or included in a traditional wild-green soup.

summary: Evergreen flowering subshrub native to the American tropics. It flowers nearly year-round in red or purple with yellow or orange centres, and its silky-haired seeds float on air currents. Broken stems and leaves release milky sap that can injure eyes.

A branching perennial herb native to South Africa’s Cape and Northern Provinces. It has tough, sparsely spined stems, small white or pinkish flowers, winter-red berries and a fibrous root mat with water-storing tubers.
edibilityNote: Eating the berries can cause diarrhea, vomiting and abdominal pain.

summary: An evergreen scrambling perennial native to southern Africa, common asparagus fern has fine, fern-like foliage clustered along tough, thorny stems. Its small berries turn from green to black and are reportedly toxic when eaten.
edibilityNote: The berries are reportedly toxic when eaten and can cause diarrhea and abdominal pain.

summary: Annual or short-lived perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region, Arabian Peninsula, Transcaucasus and Madeira. It forms a tuft of onion-like hollow leaves and bears widely spaced white or pale-pink flowers, each with a brown to reddish-purple central stripe. The flowers close at night and in overcast or low light.

A fern native to Europe, Asia and western North America, northern spleenwort grows on rocks in dense, grass-like tufts. Its long, slender leaves have narrow, leathery blades that are often forked at the tip.

A small fern occurring almost worldwide in rocky habitats, maidenhair spleenwort forms tufts of narrow evergreen fronds divided into rounded leaflets. Its dark stalks remain dark along the full length of each frond, and its several subspecies favour different rock types.

Fern native to the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. It mainly inhabits deserts, often on limestone-rich soils, and its leaflets have star-shaped scales above and hairy, spear-shaped scales beneath.
A herbaceous perennial native to southeastern Europe, forming low carpets of spoon-shaped or oval leaves. It produces showy four-petalled flowers ranging from lavender to deep pink.
An annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin and western, central and southern Asia. Its flower clusters move in the wind, and its seeds are edible.
edibilityNote: The seeds are edible.

summary: Mangrove tree native to the coasts of eastern Africa, southern Asia, Australia and northern New Zealand. It has smooth pale-grey bark, glossy green leaves with silvery-grey undersides, and upright aerial roots; its fleshy seeds often begin germinating while still on the tree.
A perennial creeping herb native to wetland areas globally. It has succulent paired leaves and small white flowers, and can grow in slightly brackish conditions.

Evergreen thorny shrub native to southern Chile and Argentina. It has orange spring flowers and purple-black summer berries; the very acidic edible fruit was consumed by Indigenous peoples in prehistoric Patagonia over millennia.
edibilityNote: The very acidic berries are edible and were consumed by Indigenous peoples in prehistoric Patagonia over millennia.

summary: A flowering shrub endemic to southern California, Nevin's barberry has dense evergreen foliage of dark green to bluish-green, spiny-toothed leaflets. Its bright yellow flowers appear in spring, followed by reddish summer berries that eventually turn dark blue.

A deciduous shrub native to central and southern Europe, southern England, northwest Africa and western Asia, European barberry has three-branched spines, yellow flowers and oblong red berries. Its sharply acidic berries are eaten fresh and traditionally used for jam and cooking, especially in southwestern Asia.
edibilityNote: The sharply acidic berries are eaten fresh and traditionally used in jam; in southwestern Asia, especially Iran, they are used in cooking.

summary: Deciduous shrub or small tree native to western North America, water birch typically grows along mountain streams. It has smooth, dark reddish-brown to nearly black bark that does not peel, and often sprouts many small limbs from its trunk.

An annual flowering plant native to much of Eurasia, North Africa and North America, three-parted beggarticks has rigid stems and fibrous roots. Its leaves are often deeply lobed, and its flower heads lack ray flowers.

A climbing shrub native to southwestern Western Australia. Its vine-like branches twine around other plants and carry hanging white, blue or pinkish flowers followed by fleshy, sausage-shaped berries. Introduced populations can become serious environmental weeds in temperate parts of southern Australia.

Perennial herb from the Mediterranean. Its leaves release a distinctive, strong tar-like smell, making the plant easy to recognize; potential uses include forage and stabilizing contaminated or degraded soils.

A flowering wetland plant native to most of Africa, Madagascar, southern Europe, the Black and Caspian Sea regions, and parts of Asia. Its nutlets and tubers are edible, and charred remains occur abundantly at Near Eastern archaeological sites from the Late Epipalaeolithic to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic.
edibilityNote: Nutlets and tubers are edible; charred remains occur at Near Eastern archaeological sites from the Late Epipalaeolithic to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic.

summary: A grass widespread across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, tor-grass typically grows in calcareous grassland. Its open flowerheads bear 10 to 15 upright spikelets, and it is an important host grass for certain insects in central Europe.
A perennial grass native across much of Europe, Asia and Africa. It commonly grows beneath forest canopies and has drooping leaves and narrow, drooping flower spikes.

A wild cabbage originating in southern Europe and North Africa, later introduced and naturalized in Australia and North America. When crushed, it smells like cabbage or broccoli. Its smooth upright stems bear pale-yellow flowers and lumpy, pea-pod-shaped fruits containing round brown seeds.

An annual mustard native to the deserts of North Africa and the Middle East, Saharan mustard has spreading stems and relatively subdued yellow flowers. When wet, its seed coats form a sticky gel that helps seeds cling to people, animals and objects. It is also used in North African cuisine, including the Libyan dish Couscous bil Aslooz.
edibilityNote: Used in North African cuisine, including the traditional Libyan dish Couscous bil Aslooz.

summary: Annual or biennial grass native to southern and central Europe. Its large, open flower clusters have branches that droop at the ends, and its spikelets turn purple as they mature.
Annual or biennial grass native to Europe, North Africa and West Asia. Its leaf sheaths are hairy, and its branched flower head usually nods and spreads.
A long-lived perennial grass native to Europe, it spreads through rhizomes and commonly forms dense sod. It begins growing in early spring and may flower again in autumn when moisture is sufficient.

An annual grass native to subarctic and temperate Eurasia, bald brome grows in moist meadows and grasslands in Europe. It has hairy leaf surfaces and branched flower clusters bearing single, many-flowered spikelets.

Vigorous arching shrub native to most of China except the far northeast. Its honey-scented lilac, purple or occasionally white flower clusters attract butterflies, but the plant can spread invasively in temperate regions.

Evergreen shrub or small tree native to South Africa and Zimbabwe, the false olive has angular, winged branchlets and leaves with smooth dark-green upper surfaces and pale, hairy undersides. Its honey-scented cream or white flowers, occasionally with reddish-orange throats, appear in spring and summer.
Annual herb native to Australia. It has yellow flowers and favours sandy or loamy places that are wet in winter, including creek lines, coastal areas and salt-lake margins.

An aquatic perennial herb native to southeastern South America and the East and West Coasts of the United States, Carolina fanwort grows rooted in the mud of still or slow-moving water. It has opposite pairs of leaves and white flowers that float on or rise above the surface.

A perennial bunchgrass of the Holarctic region, found in Eurasian wetlands and possibly introduced to Canada and the United States. It has elongated rhizomes, upright stems and flat, stiff leaf blades.

A short-lived aromatic perennial herb probably native to southern Europe, though its long cultivation leaves the precise origin unknown. It bears yellow or orange flower heads, and its edible florets are used in salads or as garnish in place of saffron.
edibilityNote: The florets are eaten in salads or as garnish and are also used to make tea.

summary: Aquatic flowering plant native to North America, from Greenland and Alaska south to Mexico. It grows almost entirely underwater in still or slow-moving wetlands, with floating stem tips and tiny flowers throughout the growing season.

A perennial aquatic plant native to Europe and North Africa, pond water-starwort favors still or slow-moving fresh or brackish water. Its submerged leaves are long and narrow while floating leaves are broader, and introduced populations can form dense mats that crowd out local vegetation.

A herbaceous perennial climber native to southern Europe, it grows strongly and spreads readily through hardy underground stems. It has large arrow-shaped leaves and showy white trumpet-shaped flowers, sometimes narrowly pink outside.

A vigorous deciduous woody vine native to eastern North America, it climbs by aerial rootlets and twining stems. Its unscented orange-to-reddish trumpet flowers have yellowish throats and generally appear after several months of warm weather.
edibilityNote: The plant is slightly toxic if ingested.

summary: An annual flowering herb indigenous to Eastern Asia and now worldwide through cultivation. It usually has separate male and female flowers, and varieties are grown for fibre, edible seed and hemp oil, or medicinal and recreational products.
edibilityNote: Seeds may be eaten raw or pressed for hempseed oil used in cooking.

summary: A biennial thistle native to Europe and Asia. It forms a flat basal rosette before producing an erect, spiny stem topped with rounded heads of threadlike purple or pink flowers, then dies after setting seed.

A usually biennial thistle native to Europe, Asia and North Africa. Its showy rose-to-violet flower heads characteristically droop when mature. Depending on climate and habitat, it can instead behave as an annual or perennial.

A flowering sedge native to Macaronesia, Europe, northwestern Africa, the Caucasus and the Middle East eastward to Turkmenistan. It is associated with disturbed, partly shaded places and is relatively moisture- and warmth-loving; introduced populations occur in parts of the Americas, New Zealand and Australia.

summary: A tussock-forming sedge native to North and Central America and parts of Eurasia, it inhabits wet forests, marshes and mountain meadows and is often associated with peat bogs. Its ridged stems bear threadlike basal leaves and star-shaped flower spikes.

Sedge native to Eurasia and eastern and western North America. It has many thin stems and narrow leaves, with open clusters of flower spikes bearing reddish or brownish bracts with gold centres and white tips.

Perennial sedge native to northern North America and widely distributed across northern temperate regions. It forms tuft-like shoots from creeping underground stems and bears glossy, bulbous fruits in long cylindrical clusters; its fibres have insulated footwear, and its underground stems were used for basketry.

A flowering plant of unstated native origin, safflower is introduced in mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira. It commonly bears yellow, orange or red flower heads and many long, sharp leaf spines. Its seeds yield cooking oil, while its flowers are occasionally used in cooking as a cheaper saffron substitute.
edibilityNote: Seed oil is used for cooking; flowers are occasionally used in cooking as a cheaper saffron substitute.

summary: A deciduous tree native to the midwestern United States, northern catalpa has an uncertain original range. It has large, heart-shaped leaves and white, trumpet-shaped flowers marked with yellow stripes and purple spots. Its long, thin brown fruit capsules often remain on the tree through winter.

A perennial shrub or small tree endemic to three California Channel Islands and Guadalupe Island in Mexico. The largest California lilac, it has large glossy leaves with felt-like undersides and plentiful bunches of bright-blue flowers, although flower colour varies among cultivated forms.

A thorny shrub native to California and Baja California, occurring in coastal and inland mountain habitats. Its grey-white waxy bark and powder-coated evergreen leaves give it a pale appearance, while older twigs harden into sharp thorns. Long-stalked clusters bear blue, lavender or white flowers.

A deciduous tree native to Southern Europe, North Africa and Asia Minor, the nettle tree has smooth grey bark with an elephant-like appearance. Its small, dark-purple fruits hang in short clusters and are sweet and edible raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: The sweet fruit is edible raw or cooked.

summary: A deciduous tree native to East Asian slopes, it has grey bark and small rounded fruits. In the Northern Hemisphere it flowers in March and April, with fruit appearing from September to October.
A clump-forming annual grass native to North and South America, it bears distinctive barbed burrs. It is invasive in coastal Australia, New Caledonia, Tahiti and Rarotonga.

An annual thistle-like plant native to Mediterranean Europe and western and Central Asia, it has a sprawling habit and downy, leathery leaves with small marginal spines. Its yellow flower heads are surrounded by numerous spiny bracts and appear from midsummer to early autumn.
edibilityNote: Bitter leaves are used to flavour alcoholic drinks; it is considered safe for food use, though large amounts may cause digestive symptoms.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to southern Italy, where it grows naturally on coastal cliffs. It produces purple flowers but is commonly cultivated for its foliage, and may grow as an annual or perennial depending on climate. Similar silvery, hairy leaves have caused frequent confusion with the unrelated Jacobaea maritima.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and introduced in the Azores. It grows in cereal fields, fallow land, roadsides and waste ground, generally on basic, nitrogen-enriched soils.

A small annual herb native to southern temperate Europe, lesser centaury lacks a basal leaf rosette when flowering. It bears a few pale pink, star-like flowers that close in the afternoon and may sometimes be reduced to one stem with a single flower.
An annual herb occurring in western Europe and northern Africa, mainly near coasts. It has opposite stalkless leaves and four, rarely five, petals that are much shorter than the sepals.

A flowering evergreen with no native origin specified in the supplied information, purple cestrum has sweet-smelling purplish-red flowers but unpleasant-smelling leaves. All parts are poisonous when ingested.
edibilityNote: All parts of the plant are poisonous when ingested.

summary: An evergreen woody shrub native to Mexico, Central America and northern South America, night jessamine has greenish-white flowers that open at night and release a powerful sweet perfume. It produces white berries and has become widely naturalized in tropical and subtropical regions.
edibilityNote: Reports are mixed: some berry ingestions caused no effects, while prolonged ingestion of green berries was associated with serious illness.

summary: A woody shrub native to Chile, with narrow leaves that smell unpleasant when crushed. It bears sprays of tubular yellow-green flowers followed by small black berries, and can lose some leaves in cool winters.
edibilityNote: All parts are reported highly toxic; ingestion has caused fatal poisoning in livestock.

summary: Large evergreen conifer native to southwestern Oregon and northwestern California, especially valleys of the Klamath Mountains and often streamside. Its foliage forms lacy, feathery, blue-green sprays with a pungent parsley-like scent. Old trees may live about 600 years.
Annual herb native to Europe and introduced to California. It has finely divided leaves and composite flowers, blooming in California between March and April.

An erect flowering shrub endemic to Western Australia. Its white or pink flowers appear from June to November and remain fresh relatively long after cutting. Its aromatic, citrus-flavoured leaves are used like rosemary in cooking or to flavour oils, sauces and spirits.
edibilityNote: The leaves are used like rosemary or infused into oil, stock, sauces, gin and other spirits for citrus flavour.

summary: An annual plant most likely native to Mediterranean and Atlantic coastal areas of southern Europe and North Africa, though its native range is uncertain. It grows low or somewhat upright, has grey-green leaves with a floury appearance, and smells strongly of rotten fish.

A perennial grass native to Africa and naturalized across tropical and subtropical regions. It spreads by creeping stems into broad stands and bears fingerlike flower clusters; it also tolerates drought and salty soils.

A flowering plant native from Central Asia west through Europe and south into Southwest Asia and North Africa. It is thin and much-branched, with small yellow, dandelion-like flowers. On Crete, leaves and tender shoots of a local variety are eaten raw or boiled in salads.
edibilityNote: On Crete, leaves and tender shoots of a local variety are eaten raw or boiled; the plant is also traditionally eaten in southern Italy.

summary: A very poisonous perennial native to North America, mainly from the Rocky Mountains westward between Alaska and California. It grows in wet places and has thick tuberous roots containing much of its toxin; internal chambers in the tubers and stem bases aid identification.
edibilityNote: Extremely poisonous to humans; ingesting green material can be fatal, and toxin is especially prevalent in the roots.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to the western Mediterranean region. It bears papery white flowers, usually marked red to maroon near the petal bases, and is coated in sticky, fragrant resin used in herbal medicine and perfumery.

An evergreen shrub native to southern Europe and northern Africa in Mediterranean forests, woodlands and scrub. Its narrow, wrinkled leaves have a hairy, glandular and sticky surface, while its flower clusters bear white five-petalled blooms.

A shrub native to the Mediterranean region, including southern Europe and parts of Western Asia and North Africa. Its wrinkled, hairy green leaves accompany white five-petalled flowers, each marked yellow at the base. It can regrow quickly after fire.
A plant in the cabbage family native to western Europe and Morocco, Coincya monensis has also been introduced to North America.

An herb native to tropical and subtropical Asia and Africa, Benghal dayflower has aerial, ground-level and underground branches bearing different flower types. Its roots and tubers are used as food; in Pakistan it is eaten as a vegetable, Nepalese people eat young leaves, and India records it as famine food.
edibilityNote: Roots and tubers are used as food; it is a vegetable in Pakistan, young leaves are eaten in Nepal, and famine use is recorded in India.

summary: Annual flowering plant native to Mediterranean Europe. Its solitary, long-stalked flowers are funnel-shaped and blue with white and yellow centres.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to New Zealand, it grows flat against exposed cliffs but may become a small tree in shelter. Its thick, exceptionally glossy leaves vary with exposure, and female plants bear orange-red fruit.
A perennial plant native to the eastern and central United States. It carries single yellow flower heads on bare stalks above mostly narrow basal leaves, and can spread into colonies.
An evergreen flowering shrub native to the Mediterranean Basin, it bears bright yellow flowers followed by slender pods. The flowers are strongly fragrant by day but almost scentless at night.

Short-lived perennial flowering plant native to Europe, the Mediterranean and Western Asia. It has aromatic, feathery bright-green foliage and abundant yellow, daisy-like flower heads in summer; its flowers were formerly used to make yellow, buff and golden-orange fabric dyes.

A low-growing shrub of unstated native origin, introduced to and naturalised in Ireland. It is cultivated in gardens and rock gardens and produces red, berry-like fruits eaten by birds, which disperse its seeds in their droppings.

A flowering plant native to Nepal, the eastern Himalayas, Assam and Myanmar, but introduced elsewhere as a garden escape. It bears shiny red fruits that ripen from September to October, following flowers in June.

Highly variable succulent native to South Africa, where it grows on rocky outcrops in grassy shrubland and the Karoo. Its grey-green leaves carry a white powdery coating, while drooping bell-shaped winter flowers are usually orange-red or salmon-orange, though yellow varieties exist.

A perennial succulent native to mountainous parts of Natal and the Eastern and Southern Cape in South Africa, it forms mats of rounded, deep-green leaves. Its white to pinkish star-shaped flowers appear in winter in its native habitat, and its flower heads can produce plantlets that fall and grow independently.

A succulent native to South Africa’s KwaZulu-Natal and Eastern Cape provinces and to Mozambique. Its thick, shiny leaves grow in opposite pairs, while older stems look woody but remain fleshy; mature plants bear small pink or white star-shaped flowers in winter.
A succulent native to southern Africa, it has woody stems and crossed pairs of green leaves that give it a miniature pine-like appearance. White flowers appear at the ends of its stems in summer.
Perennial herb native to southern Europe, including Spain, France, Italy, Malta and Greece. Each plant can produce several flower heads packed with yellow ray florets but no central disc florets.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It occupies varied dry, open habitats—including grassland, waste ground, rocky areas, open woodland and scrub—and grows on many kinds of substrate.

summary: Winter annual herb native to parts of Europe, Asia and North Africa. Its branching, ridged stem bears rough, bristly leaves that often wither by flowering, while slender purple flower heads usually produce one fruit.

An annual trailing herb with an uncertain native origin, muskmelon has many cultivated varieties. Its fruit may have sweet or bland flesh and smooth, ribbed, wrinkled or netted rind; depending on the variety, it is eaten fresh, dried or cooked, while some are grown for edible seeds.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh, dried or cooked; some varieties are cultivated for edible seeds, which may be processed into oil.

summary: A trailing or climbing annual herb native to tropical and southern Africa, paddy melon has deeply lobed leaves, small yellow flowers and small round, softly spined fruit. The entire plant is toxic to humans and several livestock species, and human poisonings have been recorded.
edibilityNote: The entire plant is toxic to humans; it has been used as an emetic, and human poisoning has been recorded.

summary: A cultivated squash domesticated in the Americas. Its forms vary dramatically in fruit shape and include pumpkins, winter squash and summer squash; many cultivated groups are edible, but ornamental gourds are not.
edibilityNote: Many cultivated groups are edible; fresh squash and blossoms are eaten, while the ornamental-gourd group is non-edible.

summary: A parasitic vine native to Eurasia and Africa, it resembles light yellow to orange-red straw wrapped tightly around its host. Its leaves are reduced to scales, and a single plant can produce more than 10,000 seeds at once.

Parasitic plant thought to be native to North America. Its thin, pale green or yellow stems wrap around many kinds of herbaceous host, penetrating them with nutrient-absorbing organs; seedlings die if they cannot find a host.

Taprooted branching herb of unstated native origin, found worldwide in warm-temperate to tropical regions. It has threadlike green leaves and small rounded flower clusters; an 1889 account warned that plants grown in damp soils may be acrid and injurious.

A cactus native to Southern California and Baja California. It is mostly erect and tree-like, with narrow gray-green segments bearing many brown or reddish spines; its reddish-purple flowers are often carried on fruits from previous seasons.
A short-lived perennial grass found across most of Europe and southwest Asia and introduced elsewhere. Its seed head is flat on one side, while its glossy, keeled leaves cluster near the base.

An annual or perennial sedge native in some regions of the United States and widespread across much of the world, yellow nutsedge has triangular stems and produces hard underground tubers. The sweet, nutty tubers are eaten raw or cooked, but are generally soaked to soften them; they are also made into flour and drinks.
edibilityNote: The tubers are eaten raw or cooked, usually after soaking to soften them, and are also made into flour and sweet drinks.

summary: Flowering sedge native to North America, South America, Europe, Asia and Africa, with a cosmopolitan distribution; it was introduced to parts of Australia.
An annual sedge native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it grows in wet places such as swamps and river margins. Its paper-thin stems carry clusters of flat, dark-brown to deep-purple flower spikes.

Perennial sedge with no native origin specified in the supplied information. It is widespread across tropical and subtropical regions, favoring brackish water and other saline or alkaline wetlands. It can form rhizome-linked clumps and bears cylindrical spikelets ranging from green to reddish or dark brown.

Perennial sedge native to Africa, southern and central Europe, and southern Asia. It forms chains of underground tubers that enable rapid regrowth and make it a highly invasive weed. Its bitter tubers are edible, and the plant serves as a staple carbohydrate for some tropical hunter-gatherers and as famine food in some agrarian cultures.
edibilityNote: Bitter tubers are edible; the plant is a staple carbohydrate for some tropical hunter-gatherers and a famine food in some agrarian cultures, including Rajasthan.

summary: Perennial fern native to eastern Asia. It grows in moist, stable places such as coastal cliff crevices, stream banks and rocky slopes. Its long leaves carry pairs of shiny, leathery bright-green leaflets with netlike veins.

A shrub native to the Iberian Peninsula, especially western Portugal and western Spain. It has many flexible branches and white, pea-like flowers, while its hairy pods turn black and burst open to scatter their seeds.

Upright, bushy shrub native to the western Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Morocco. Its green stems have lengthwise ridges, while its densely hairy pods darken as they ripen and release their seeds explosively.
A grass native to Africa and Asia, Durban crowfoot creeps along the ground and produces straight shoots. It mostly grows in heavy soils at damp sites.
edibilityNote: Reported as a traditional famine grain in Africa, though the source flags this claim as needing citation.

summary: A perennial tussock grass native to Europe and adjacent parts of Asia and North Africa, it may also be native to Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. Its stems lie along the ground before turning upward, bearing narrow hairy leaves and silvery-green or purplish flower clusters in summer.

A hardy deciduous flowering shrub native to cool temperate and subarctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere. It has finely hairy foliage, peeling bark on older stems and usually pale to bright yellow, buttercup-shaped flowers, though some western Chinese populations have orange to reddish petals.

An annual herb native to the Americas. Its ripe red-brown fruit bears unusually long spines, while its broad, irregularly toothed leaves are softly hairy. Every part contains dangerous toxins and may be fatal if eaten by humans or other animals.
edibilityNote: All plant parts contain dangerous toxins and may be fatal if eaten by humans.

summary: A biennial flowering herb native to temperate Afro-Eurasia. It has finely divided, lacy leaves and dense white flower clusters, often with a single red or purple central flower.
edibilityNote: Young roots are described as edible before becoming woody; flowers are sometimes battered and fried, while leaves and seeds are also edible.

summary: A perennial tufted grass native to North America, Central Africa, eastern Australia, New Zealand and Eurasia. Its deeply grooved, dark-green leaf surface feels rough and may cut in one direction but feels smooth in the other.
A compact evergreen perennial native to Austria, Croatia and Slovenia. It bears pink flowers with five fringed petals from May through August.
A low-growing perennial native to Texas, Mexico and the Caribbean. It prefers wetter soils and was once recommended as a low-maintenance lawn substitute, but proved vulnerable to flea beetles.

An annual grass believed to have originated in Asia, tropical finger-grass now occurs throughout the tropics and many temperate regions. It roots at its stem joints and sends out runners, rapidly forming untidy patches; in some countries it is an aggressive invasive weed.

An annual grass native to Europe and Asia, now introduced across much of the warm temperate world as a common roadside and garden weed. Its narrow, branched flower heads bear tiny spikelets that darken to purple, while spreading stems may root at their joints.

Perennial ornamental shrub native to a small area of South Africa’s Eastern Cape. Its daisy-like flowers have white rays, reddish-blue undersides and dark blue or purple centres, and it can remain evergreen.
Perennial herb native to coastal South Africa. Known as the trailing African daisy, it has become a widespread coastal weed in New Zealand, particularly on the North Island.

An annual flowering plant native to southern Africa, particularly western South Africa and Namibia. It grows in winter-rainfall areas and sandy deserts, flowering in early spring with generally yellow or orange heads marked with purple.

A flowering plant native to temperate North Africa, Europe and parts of western Asia, annual wall-rocket is annual but sometimes perennial. It has a basal rosette of lobed leaves, usually yellow flowers and long fruit capsules, and often grows on disturbed ground.

A mustard-family herb native to Europe and western Asia. Its deeply divided, often fleshy leaves have a peppery taste and musty smell; cultivated baby leaves are eaten in mixed salads and sold as wild rocket or arugula.
edibilityNote: Cultivated baby leaves are eaten as salad greens, often in mixed salads and marketed as wild rocket or arugula.

summary: Fern native to much of temperate Europe, Asia and North America. Its upright, semi-evergreen leaves form a single crown, with orange-brown scales on their stalks; mature leaves release spores from August to November.
edibilityNote: The rhizomes are toxic; excessive doses can cause serious poisoning, blindness or death.

summary: A rare succulent endemic to coastal mesas in southwestern San Diego County, California, it has exceptionally small leaves that are often almost buried. Its leaves disappear toward summer, and after flowering all above-ground traces may vanish while a starch-rich base survives underground.

An uncommon perennial succulent native to coastal locations in southern California and Baja California. Its fleshy, mostly green, strap-shaped leaves form rosettes, and white five-petalled flowers appear from April through June.

An annual or short-lived perennial herb native to the Americas, Mexican tea has irregular branches, long narrow leaves and small green flowers. Its strongly aromatic leaves are used as a vegetable, seasoning and herbal tea, but overdoses of its essential oil have caused deaths.
edibilityNote: Leaves, preferably collected before seeding, are used as a vegetable, seasoning and herbal tea; the concentrated essential oil can be fatal.

summary: A flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region, Jerusalem oak is a hardy annual with a strong scent reminiscent of stock cubes. It can be used as a flavouring in cooking.
edibilityNote: Used as a flavouring in cooking.

summary: An annual herb native to South America and introduced across most continents. Its branching stems may grow upright or along the ground, bearing small, lobed, glandular leaves and dense clusters of tiny flowers.
Aromatic annual herb native to Australia. Its stems and leaves are sticky and gland-covered, while tiny green flowers form dense spherical clusters beside the leaves.

Wild grass originating in tropical Asia. It is the wild ancestor of sawa millet, although some taxonomists combine the wild and domesticated forms. In India, its seeds are prepared as khichdi and eaten during festival fasting days.
edibilityNote: In India, seeds are cooked as khichdi for festival fasts; historically in Australia, seeds were pounded, mixed with water and made into bread.

summary: A glandular, woolly perennial herb native to Eurasia. Its hairy stems carry leaves that are sticky above and white-woolly below, topped by nearly spherical heads of white or blue-grey flowers.
Flowering plant endemic to La Palma in the Canary Islands, where it grows in laurel forests. It lives for two or three years, producing a towering cone of small blue flowers only once before dying.

Winter annual plant native to western and southern Europe, northern Africa and southwestern Asia. It has rough, hairy leaves and purple flowers on branched spikes, and is invasive in several introduced regions.

A flowering plant native to North and South America, false daisy commonly grows in moist warm-temperate to tropical places. It has hairy opposite leaves and small white flower heads. In Southeast Asia, Balinese people cook it as a vegetable, while Javanese people eat the herb as part of lalap.
edibilityNote: Balinese people cook it as a vegetable; Javanese people eat the herb as part of lalap.

summary: Variable perennial grass native to South Africa, Lesotho and Namibia. Its flower clusters begin pale and darken to purple or reddish with age, and it may or may not spread by underground stems. Outside its native range it sometimes becomes a noxious or invasive weed.
An annual spikesedge widely distributed across Canada and the United States. It grows in wet places and rice paddies, with weak, spongy cylindrical stems topped by rounded or oblong flower spikes.

A mat-forming perennial sedge of wetlands across Europe, North Africa, northern and central Asia, and North America. Common spikerush is extremely variable worldwide and difficult to distinguish from closely related species.

A perennial wetland herb of unstated native origin, small spikerush occurs widely but patchily across several continents in brackish and saltwater marshes and mudflats. It forms short tufts of spongy stems from a distinctive J-shaped or horseshoe-shaped tuber.

summary: A small annual grass distributed across warmer parts of the world, it is a troublesome weed of crops, lawns and golf courses and can set seed even when closely mown. Its seeds are edible and sometimes used as famine food, though yields are low.
edibilityNote: The seeds are edible and sometimes used as famine food, but yields are low.

summary: A grass native to South America. It occurs in disturbed ground and farmland and is introduced in the Azores and Madeira.

summary: Perennial aquatic plant native to most of North America. It lives entirely underwater except for small surface-floating flowers, with bright translucent leaves usually arranged three around each stem. In favourable conditions it grows rapidly and can choke shallow waterways.
Perennial horsetail widespread across cooler Eurasia and North America. Its wind-carried spores bear four long ribbon-like structures, and the plant can also spread through runners.
edibilityNote: Some sources consider it safe in moderate amounts when properly cooked, although it is poisonous to mammals and heat may denature its thiaminases.

summary: A flowering grass native to the western Mediterranean. A memorable feature is the broad, pale-yellow glandular ring on the stem below the flower head; smaller flower clusters often occur lower on the stem.

summary: Annual bunchgrass native to much of Eurasia and Africa. Its tufted stems and long leaves bear glandular tissue, and the plant has a strong scent.
A usually long-lived perennial grass native to southern Africa, though some forms are annual. It forms stem tufts with narrow, drooping leaves and an exceptionally dense, deep-spreading root network.
edibilityNote: Documented as used for food in Lesotho, though the plant part and preparation are unspecified.

summary: An annual grass found from North America south to Argentina, often on disturbed ground or dry hills and mountains. It forms dense tufts with slender stems and open flower clusters bearing straw-coloured or orange spikelets, sometimes tinged purple.

A grass native to most of the subtropical and warm-temperate Old World, it commonly grows in disturbed sandy or gravelly places, including pavement cracks and rail embankments. Its tiny edible seeds are difficult to harvest and are usually regarded as famine food.
edibilityNote: The small seeds are edible but difficult to harvest and handle, so they are usually regarded as famine food.

summary: An annual tuft-forming grass native to the Americas from Canada to Argentina. It grows in varied open habitats and has spreading flower branches bearing yellowish to purplish spikelets.

An annual grass native to Eurasia and Africa, with uncertain native status in North America. It has narrow leaves, often scattered glandular pits and open flower clusters with whorled lower branches; its grain is edible and has occasionally been harvested in Ethiopia only in times of desperation.
edibilityNote: The grain is edible; it has occasionally been harvested in Ethiopia during times of desperation.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to Portugal, Spain and southwestern France, densely clothed in short, leathery, needle-like leaves. Hanging bells of pale pink to white flowers appear in winter and spring, followed by tiny wind-dispersed seeds.

An annual or sometimes biennial flowering herb native to North and Central America, annual fleabane has numerous leaves, with lower ones often coarsely toothed or cleft. Its flower heads have yellow centres and rays ranging from white to pale lavender.

A tropical and subtropical pioneer plant, it most likely originates from Central or South America, although its precise origin is unknown. Its narrow leaves are covered with stiff hairs, while its flower heads combine white outer florets with yellow central florets.

An annual herb native throughout most of North and Central America and widely naturalized in Eurasia and Australia. It bears dense clusters of small white or pale purple and yellow flower heads, produces many wind-dispersed seeds, and was the first weed reported to develop glyphosate resistance.

A perennial flowering herb native to much of the western United States, where scattered populations grow in moist forests and meadows. Its flower heads have golden-yellow centres surrounded by as many as 140 white florets.

A spreading perennial flowering plant native to much of Mexico, Central America, Colombia and Venezuela. It grows from woody rhizomes and bears daisy-like flowers with golden-yellow centres and white to pinkish rays. In the UK, it flowers from May to October.

An annual or biennial herb native to eastern and central North America, extending west to Manitoba, Idaho and Texas. Its hairy leaves occur mainly low on the plant, while branching stems may carry as many as 200 small flower heads with white, pink or blue rays around yellow centres.

An annual herb, though perennial in South Africa’s Western Cape, probably native to South America and widely naturalised across tropical and subtropical regions. It has white flowers and small, straw-coloured, dandelion-like seed heads.
An annual or biennial herb native to the Mediterranean region of southern Europe, northern Africa and southwest Asia. It has hairy leaves and small purplish flowers with soft, spine-tipped sepals.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. In Portugal it grows on fallow ground and path verges.
