summary: A eucalypt tree endemic to limited areas of southern South Australia, sugar gum occurs naturally in the Flinders Ranges, Eyre Peninsula and Kangaroo Island. Its smooth grey old bark sheds in irregular patches to reveal yellow to orange fresh bark, and creamy-white summer flowers cluster on leafless branchlets within the crown.
A small, bushy tree endemic to the southern coast of Western Australia. It has smooth whitish-grey bark, while its flower buds fuse into clusters and its fruits form a woody mass.

A small to medium-sized tree endemic to Tasmania, particularly its southeastern lowlands. It has smooth white or pale grey bark, sometimes fibrous on older trunks, with narrow linear leaves, clusters of white flowers and woody cup-shaped fruit.

A small to medium-sized tree endemic to eastern Australia, red ironbark has dark, deeply furrowed bark. Its flowers may be white, red, pink or creamy yellow, followed by woody, cup-shaped to nearly spherical fruit.

A tree endemic to southeastern Australia, manna gum has smooth pale bark that often peels in long ribbons, white flowers and woody cup-shaped fruit. Its bark produces a sweet, white, crumbly manna valued by Aboriginal people.

A small tree or large shrub native to the Mediterranean region, tree spurge grows on protected, sunny mountainsides because it is frost-sensitive. Its white, sticky sap is toxic and has been applied to skin growths in traditional medicine since ancient times.

A spurge native to western China, Kyrgyzstan and Pakistan, caper spurge is usually biennial but occasionally annual, with waxy blue-green stems and paired leaves. All parts, including the seeds and roots, are poisonous, and its latex may irritate skin.
edibilityNote: All parts, including seeds and roots, are poisonous to humans; toxins may also pass into milk from goats that eat it.

summary: A perennial herb native to Mediterranean-climate regions of northern Africa, temperate Asia and parts of Europe. It has broad leaves and small three-lobed fruits, while its milky sap is toxic to humans and may irritate the skin, eyes and digestive tract.
edibilityNote: The plant is toxic to humans; exposure to its milky sap may irritate the digestive tract.

summary: Flowering herb native from the southern United States and West Indies south to Mexico and Belize. It bears large purple, bell-shaped flowers through the growing season, especially from spring into summer. It inhabits wet alkaline or coastal places and tolerates salt winds well.

A woody flowering vine native to Asia, including China, Russia and Kazakhstan. Its climbing stems carry pointed oval or nearly triangular leaves and branching clusters of white flowers. The flowers may become pale or bright pink as the shiny black fruit develops.

A fast-growing annual vine native throughout Europe, Asia and northern Africa. Its stems twine clockwise, bearing triangular leaves, inconspicuous greenish flowers and small triangular fruits; the edible seeds were formerly grown as food and occur in Bronze Age remains.
edibilityNote: The seeds are edible and were formerly a food crop; remains have been found in Bronze Age middens.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira. It grows on salty soils, coastal sand and gravel, beside saltworks roads and, more rarely, in enclosed brackish depressions.

Perennial flowering plant native to temperate and subarctic parts of the Northern Hemisphere. It dies back each winter, spreads into colonies through underground stems, and bears leaves in groups of four around square stems.
edibilityNote: It has a sweet smell and taste and can be eaten as a wild salad green.

summary: Small annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, Black Sea region and Macaronesia. It has thin, spreading stems, pointed leaves arranged in whorls, white flowers and smooth nutlet fruits.

Herbaceous perennial from Europe, North Africa, Siberia’s Altay region and the Caucasus, hedge bedstraw has square stems with rising branches. Small, white, four-petalled flowers appear from May to September in the Northern Hemisphere.

Annual flowering herb native to South America and the southeastern United States, from Texas and Oklahoma to Virginia but not Florida. It has long, narrow leaves clustered near the base and many small flower heads with purple central flowers.

Annual flowering herb native to South America. Its woolly-haired leaves appear light green, and it bears elongated clusters of small flower heads, each with a few purple disc flowers and no ray flowers.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it also occurs as an introduced species in Madeira.
An annual grass native to mainland Portugal and introduced to the Azores and Madeira. In Portugal it grows in moist meadows and traditionally irrigated grasslands.

A shrub native to southwestern Europe, North Africa and the Canary Islands. It has hairy green stems, tough narrow leaflets with woolly undersides, and dense clusters of bright yellow, pea-like flowers.

An annual herb found throughout Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, and introduced to North America, long-stalked crane's-bill has deeply cut leaves resembling a pigeon's foot. Its pink-to-purple flowers have five distinctly veined petals.

A herbaceous annual native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa, it has glossy rounded or kidney-shaped leaves and brittle, often red stems. Paired bright-pink flowers appear from May to August, and the whole plant tends to turn red.
An evergreen perennial native to Madeira. It forms a rosette of divided, fan-shaped leaves and bears pink flowers on long red stems.

Perennial plant of unspecified native origin. It grows along roadside verges and hedgerows and is probably introduced in England and Wales; it is also found in the southern Alps, Pyrenees and Caucasus.
An annual herb native across temperate Europe, northern Africa and southwestern Asia. It has rounded, shallowly lobed basal leaves and small pink flowers whose petals are only shallowly notched.
A perennial spreading herb native to Australia and New Zealand. Its stems are coarsely hairy, its swollen taproot is often turnip-like, and its pink flowers frequently have yellowish veins.

Summer-flowering coastal plant native to Europe, northern Africa, Macaronesia and temperate western Asia. It has bluish-grey, waxy leaves, bright yellow or orange flowers and distinctive upright, horn-shaped seed capsules.
edibilityNote: All parts, including the seeds, are toxic and can cause severe symptoms or death if eaten.

summary: A herbaceous annual flowering plant probably native only to the eastern Mediterranean. It bears deeply lobed leaves and bright-yellow flower heads, and its long flowering period makes it a particularly valuable nectar source for insects.
edibilityNote: In Crete and Greece, leaves and tender shoots of the neromantilida variety are eaten raw in salads or browned in hot olive oil.

summary: Annual flowering herb native to Eurasia and Africa, Hairy Carpet Weed has prostrate to somewhat upright stems covered in felt-like whitish hairs. Its oval or spade-shaped leaves grow in whorls, and its small clustered flowers have woolly sepals but no petals.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and stems are used as a vegetable in some tropical countries.

summary: A wetland grass native to mainland Portugal and Madeira and introduced to the Azores. It grows in ponds, marshes and other waterlogged places and is notably blue-green, with a sparsely branched flower head and often dark-violet anthers.

summary: A perennial grass native to Europe, the Mediterranean region and Western Asia, water manna grass grows in wet places such as ditches, riverbanks and ponds. It has creeping rootstocks and long, pale-green leaves that often fold along the keel and lie on the water; historically, its grains were cooked as gruel and used in other European dishes.
edibilityNote: Historically in Europe, the grains were cooked as gruel and used in cakes, flatbreads, dumplings, soups and sausages.

summary: A fibre crop native from Mexico to Ecuador and northeastern Brazil, parts of the Caribbean, and several Pacific islands. Its cultivars account for about 90% of global cotton production, and its varieties differ notably in fibre length.

A tree endemic to eastern Australia, the silk oak has deeply divided leaves and golden-yellow to orange flowers with red blotches. Indigenous Australians traditionally consumed its rich nectar directly from the blossom or shaken into water, although the flowers and fruit contain toxic hydrogen cyanide.
edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians traditionally consumed flower nectar directly or shaken into water; the flowers and fruit contain toxic hydrogen cyanide.

summary: A large-leaved flowering perennial native to southern Chile and neighboring parts of Argentina and Bolivia, it has huge lobed leaves and spike-covered stems. In Chile, peeled stalks are eaten fresh or cooked into jam or cordial, while the leaves are used to prepare curanto.
edibilityNote: In native Chile, peeled stalks are eaten fresh or cooked into jam or cordial; leaves are used to prepare curanto.

summary: An ornamental annual native to Asia and Europe.

An herbaceous perennial native to central and eastern Europe, it forms branching mounds covered in clouds of tiny white summer flowers. It naturally grows on dry, sandy or stony steppes, often over calcareous soil. It is described as toxic to humans and can cause contact dermatitis.

A perennial flowering plant native to the Himalayas, Sichuan and northern Vietnam. It tolerates deep shade, and even small rhizome fragments can regrow after crushing, seawater immersion or years out of soil.

A trailing evergreen subshrub native to South Africa’s Cape Provinces, Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe, licorice plant has furry grey-green leaves, small white flowers and a faint licorice aroma. Despite its name, it is not closely related to the true liquorice used for candy.

A clumping perennial herb native to South America, especially Argentina, fragrant heliotrope has branching hairy stems and abundant, wavy-edged leaves. Its curved flower spikes carry tiny bright-purple blooms with tubular yellow throats.

An annual herb native to Eurasia and North Africa, European heliotrope has soft-haired stems and leaves, with coiled spikes of fragrant white flowers. It contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids and is poisonous.
edibilityNote: The plant contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids and is described as poisonous.

summary: A cypress tree endemic to the Santa Cruz Mountains of west-central California. Its seed cones remain closed on the tree until heat from fire opens them, allowing new seedlings to emerge afterward. The species is federally listed as threatened.

A medium-sized evergreen conifer endemic to California, it survives naturally in only two small stands near Carmel. Strong coastal winds often give it an irregular, flat-topped shape, while its dense bright-green foliage releases a deep lemony scent when crushed.

An annual native to the Old World tropics and subtropics, flower-of-an-hour bears white or yellow flowers with purple centres. Its unripe seedpods resemble pale green paper lanterns with purple highlights.

An aquatic perennial occurring across Eurasia and North America, including Greenland, the Tibetan Plateau and Arizona. It creeps through shallow water and mudflats, rooting underwater while most leaves rise above the surface; submerged leaves become thinner, limper and longer, especially in deeper streams.

A rhizomatous perennial grass native to Europe and North Africa, creeping velvet grass grows in woods and hedgerows. Disturbed rhizome fragments can produce fresh shoots, and its hairy stem joints help distinguish it from similar grass.
Annual herb native to the temperate Northern Hemisphere. It has white flowers and may trail along the ground or grow upright.

Perennial grass native to much of Africa and Eurasia. It forms tough, dense clumps from underground stems and bears hairy spikelets with bent bristles. In South Africa it is widely used for thatching, and it is also used for livestock grazing and weaving.

A shrub native to western Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, tutsan has red-tinted oval leaves and bright yellow flowers. Its berries turn from red to black yet remain soft and fleshy when ripe, unlike those of related species.

A low, creeping evergreen shrub native to the Strandzha Mountains along the Bulgarian and Turkish Black Sea coast. It has opposite green leaves and rich yellow, rose-like flowers with numerous stamens. Underground stems let it spread rapidly, and it has invasive potential in some parts of California.

A flowering shrub endemic to the Canary Islands and Madeira, it grows in dry scrub and forested slopes. It has waxy, lance-shaped leaves and plentiful bright to deep yellow flowers with many whiskery stamens.
A herbaceous annual flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region. It has erect leafy flowering branches and clusters of white, pink, or purple flowers, blooming from May through June.

An annual herb native to the Himalayas, particularly Kashmir and surrounding areas, it bears pink or lavender flowers with a long white spur. Its ripe fruits burst and can launch seeds several metres.

Bulb-forming herbaceous perennial native to Argentina and Uruguay. Its shiny, grasslike leaves smell of onion when crushed, while each spring stem bears one honey-scented, star-shaped flower ranging from nearly white to deep purple-blue.

Perennial climbing herb of uncertain native origin, possibly spanning Cape Verde to the Arabian Peninsula through Africa and the Mediterranean. It has deeply divided leaves, bulbous roots and large white-to-lavender funnel-shaped flowers.
edibilityNote: Most parts are reportedly edible; roots are eaten cooked and young leaves are eaten, though ingestion can cause respiratory symptoms.

summary: A vigorous, long-lived perennial vine whose exact native range is unclear, though most authorities place it in the Neotropics. It has heart-shaped or three-lobed leaves and funnel-shaped flowers that shift from bright blue in the morning to deep pink by day’s end. Grown ornamentally, it is invasive in many regions.

A flowering plant native to the steppe and desert zones of the Caucasus, Central Asia through Eastern Siberia, and Western Asia. Its leaves yield a blue dye that was once important across Europe and is still used by craft dyers.

A mat-forming perennial sedge native to Eurasia and Africa, and possibly Australasia, it inhabits moist or wet ground, often near coasts. Its very thin grooved stems bear one tiny spikelet, or a cluster of up to three, beside a stiff bract extending beyond the flowers.

A perennial flowering plant native to South Africa's Cape Provinces. It has twisting basal leaves and a dense, showy spike of usually orange or yellow flowers, often spotted; cultivated plants vary in colour through breeding.

A subtropical tree native to south-central South America. It is remembered for abundant, long-lasting violet flowers followed by tough woody pods with many flat, winged seeds, and it is considered Vulnerable in its native range.

A perennial rush native to the Americas, northern and southern Africa, western and southern Europe, and West Asia, spiny rush grows in wet habitats including bogs, meadows and salt marshes. Its stems and leaves form a rounded tussock and end in stiff, sharp points.
A perennial rush native to Eurasia, Canada, Greenland and much of the United States. It grows in moist ground and has hollow, flattened leaves whose internal crosswise partitions can be seen or felt.

A small evergreen tree native to Australia, specifically Norfolk Island, eastern Queensland and Lord Howe Island. It has a usually pyramidal form and waxy pale-pink to mauve flowers. Its hairy capsules contain hairs that itch on contact with skin.

summary: A strongly scented trailing shrub native to South America, specifically Uruguay, parts of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay and southern Brazil, it forms dense ground-covering mats and can root where its stems touch soil. It bears rounded clusters of purple, lavender and white flowers, followed by poisonous fleshy fruits.
edibilityNote: The fleshy drupes are poisonous.

summary: Annual herb native to southern Europe and North Africa, with a winged, hairless stem and very narrow paired leaflets. It bears tiny coiling tendrils, solitary purple pea flowers and hairless pods that split open.

An annual climbing plant native to Sicily, southern Italy and the Aegean Islands. Its leaf-tip tendrils twine around supports, while its usually strongly scented flowers are purple in the wild but vary widely in cultivated forms.
A perennial wild pea native to Europe, Asia and North America. Its leaves are divided into oval or oblong leaflets, with branched, coiling tendrils and clusters of pinkish-purple pea flowers.

A tiny floating aquatic plant native to the southern United States, Mexico and some Caribbean islands, lesser duckweed grows in quiet, still waters. Its green fronds generally have three veins, and its rapid reproduction has helped it become established or invasive beyond its native range.

Floating freshwater flowering plant native across northern Europe through Japan and in North America. It usually reproduces without seeds and has up to four small leaves, each with one dangling root; it can also produce starch-filled resting fronds that sink and remain dormant until conditions improve.

A usually biennial mustard-family plant native to Europe and invasive in North America. Its white flowers give way to flat oval seedpods; young leaves are eaten raw or boiled, while young fruits and seeds provide a pepper-and-mustard-like spice.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw or boiled; young fruits and seeds are used as a spice.

summary: A low, sprawling annual herb, rarely biennial, native to parts of Africa, western Asia and Europe. It has deeply divided leaves and small, wart-like fruits; it was formerly eaten in salads as a poor-quality watercress substitute.
edibilityNote: Formerly eaten in salads as a watercress substitute, but judged poor quality and reportedly tasting slightly of mustard.

summary: An annual or biennial herb likely native to North America, common peppergrass has a short, upright, branching stem and a basal rosette of leaves. Its dense clusters of tiny flowers usually lack petals, and its flattened fruits have shallow notches.

A perennial flowering plant native to temperate western Europe. Its stalked basal leaves differ markedly from the triangular stem leaves, and its small white flowers are followed by smooth, distinctly beaked capsules.

An annual or biennial mustard-family herb native to much of North America and Central America. Its branched flower clusters resemble bottlebrushes, bearing small white flowers followed by greenish fruits. Young leaves are eaten raw or cooked, while young seedpods serve as a black-pepper substitute.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw, sautéed or as a cooked green; young seedpods are used as a black-pepper substitute.

summary: A perennial herb endemic to Portugal, occurring along the western mainland coast and in the Azores. It grows beside streams, ditches and lagoons, and the mainland population is assessed as Critically Endangered.

summary: A perennial herb native to France and Spain, with large, toothed leaves around its base. Its daisy-like flower heads have white outer petals surrounding a densely packed yellow centre.

An evergreen perennial native to southern Oregon and northern California, where it grows in rocky subalpine mountain habitat. Its thick, fleshy leaves form a basal rosette, while spring-to-summer flowers range from striped pale pink or white to solid orange or yellow.
Evergreen shrub or small tree native to central and southern Japan and Korea. It has thick, glossy leaves, white flower clusters and oval fruits that ripen purple-black with a waxy bloom.
An evergreen tree native to southern China. It has glossy dark-green leaves and strongly fragrant white or near-white flowers, though some people find the scent unpleasant.

Dense, fast-growing shrub or small tree native to Japan and Korea. It is deciduous but may remain evergreen or semi-evergreen in warm-winter areas, bearing pungently scented white flowers followed by purple-black fruits that are poisonous to humans.
edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous if eaten by humans; the purple-black fruits are specifically identified as poisonous.

summary: Perennial herb native to the coasts of the Canary Islands. It forms a basal rosette of thick leaves and stiff, branching clusters of small flowers with lavender sepals and white petals.
Salt-tolerant sea lavender native to the Mediterranean region. It excretes salt through glands on its flower clusters, produces many seeds and has become invasive in California salt marshes.

Short-lived perennial native to the Mediterranean Basin, usually growing in sandy ground and often treated as an annual. Its summer flowers form papery clusters in white, pink, purple or yellow and can be used in dried arrangements.

summary: Perennial herb native to central and southern Italy, including Sicily, purple toadflax has upright stems topped with clusters of flowers. Its flowers are usually dark purple or violet, rarely pale or white, and bloom from April to October.

An annual herb native across much of the Americas, from Canada to Chile, yellowseed false pimpernel grows in wet places such as riverbanks, pond margins and meadows. Its small white tubular flowers have a blue or purple tint, and its capsules contain yellow seeds.

An annual herb native to Algeria and Tunisia. It has waxy, narrow leaves and five red petals surrounding stamens with light-blue pollen. Although occasionally recorded far beyond its established range, including the British Isles, it rarely persists there for more than one season.

A low, scrambling flowering perennial native to southern Africa. Wild plants have blue-to-violet flowers with a fan-shaped lower lip, while garden varieties offer many colors and are often grown as annual edging or basket plants in temperate regions.

A deciduous perennial climber native to Southern Europe, Western Asia and North Africa, it bears dense flower spikes above paired, fused leaves. Its long tubular flowers range from pale yellow to reddish pink, followed by bright red poisonous berries.
edibilityNote: The berries are poisonous; documented leaf and flower use is animal fodder, not human food.

summary: Twining vine native to East Asia, including many parts of China. Its vanilla-scented flowers open white and fade to yellow, followed by black berries in autumn. It has become invasive in numerous countries.
edibilityNote: Flowers and their sweet nectar are eaten; all parts except the flower nectar may be toxic in very large quantities.

summary: A bushy shrub native to Siberia and other parts of eastern Asia, especially China. It bears sweet-smelling white, pink or crimson flowers and shiny orange or red berries; eating the berries is not recommended because they can cause diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain.
edibilityNote: The berries are mildly poisonous to humans; eating them may cause diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain.

summary: An annual plant of unstated native origin, slender bird's-foot-trefoil is widely distributed from Macaronesia to Xinjiang. It forms ground-hugging mats and has hairy red stems, single yellow flowers and distinctive reddish seeds.

Flowering pea-family plant native to western and southern Europe and southwest Asia. It tolerates salty, poor soil and has naturalised in many other places, including Argentina’s Pampas and parts of the United States.

An aquatic plant whose native origin is not supplied, it forms dense mats along pond margins and can outcompete other plants. It produces viable seeds but also reproduces very effectively through vegetative growth, while its large, showy flowers attract many kinds of insects.

A mat-forming perennial flowering herb native to parts of the Americas, creeping primrose-willow has stems that root where their nodes touch wet ground. It bears opposite leaves and tiny yellow, four-petalled flowers, and is also cultivated as an aquarium plant.

A deciduous woody shrub native to China, it now ranges across Asia and southeastern Europe. Its weak arching branches often bear short, leafless spines, and its bright orange-red fruit is the main variety of goji berry.

A small club moss with a circumpolar northern distribution across Eurasia and North America, from Arctic to mountain temperate regions. It forms ground-hugging patches whose horizontal stems root at intervals, while short upright spore-bearing stems appear in July and August. It inhabits wet places such as bogs, ponds and damp tundra.

summary: A prostrate annual herb native to Europe, it often grows in moist places such as marshes. Its reddish stem roots where it touches wet earth, while its fleshy, spoon-shaped leaves accompany tiny flowers that may have white or pink petals or none.

An annual flowering herb native to Europe and introduced in parts of western North America, often growing in moist places such as ponds. Its branching stems bear small flower clusters with bright red glandular sepals and tiny lavender petals.

A succulent perennial flowering plant native to Southern Africa, coppery mesemb forms a low, spreading groundcover whose woody stems root wherever they touch suitable ground. Its waxy, water-filled leaves accompany flowers with narrow red, orange and yellow petals, sometimes purple underneath.

A shrubby annual, biennial or perennial native to the coasts of western Europe and the Mediterranean, tree mallow bears dark pink to purple flowers in clusters. It tolerates seawater and usually grows on exposed coasts and small islands. Its seeds are edible; some sources also describe the hairy leaves as edible but unpalatable unless finely cut.
edibilityNote: Seeds are edible; some sources describe the leaves as edible but unpleasantly hairy unless cut very thinly.

summary: An annual herb that may persist as a biennial or perennial in favourable conditions, dwarf mallow is native to most of the Old World except sub-Saharan Africa. It grows low to the ground, with downy, kidney-shaped or shallowly lobed leaves and small flower clusters partly hidden by the leaves.
edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; stalks are also edible, and seeds were formerly ground into flour in times of need.

summary: An annual or biennial mallow originating in Asia. It has small white, pink or red flowers, and its leaves were an important vegetable in pre-Han China, though cultivation and consumption later dwindled.
edibilityNote: The leaves were widely cultivated as a vegetable in pre-Han China; consumption had become rare by the Ming dynasty.

summary: A perennial herb native to Southern California and northern Baja California, it grows from a huge, hard tuber and sends up vines after winter rain. It bears green prickly fruit that turn yellow and rupture as they ripen, releasing large seeds, before the plant dies back completely in summer.
edibilityNote: All parts are toxic and were not traditionally consumed.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to southern and eastern Europe, German chamomile has fragrant flower heads with white rays, yellow centres and a hollow base. Its flower oil is characteristically blue, and the plant is commonly used to make tea.
edibilityNote: The plant is commonly used to make chamomile tea.

summary: A flowering plant native to southern Europe from Spain to Greece, hoary stock commonly grows on coastal cliffs or old walls. Its garden forms produce strongly scented flowers in colours ranging from white and cream to red, purple, or blue. Varieties may be grown as annuals, biennials, or, for Maltese stock, perennials.

A perennial native to the western Mediterranean, including parts of North Africa and Spain, it is a dwarf ornamental with small white flower heads surrounding yellow centres. Its flowers open when sunlight reaches them.

An evergreen tree native to southern South America, including Chile, Argentina, Bolivia and southern Brazil. It has small, finely toothed leaves and yellow capsules containing seeds wrapped in a red membrane; the tree grows slowly and resists drought.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It grows in rocky grassland, scrub clearings and rock crevices, favouring dry, stony and often alkaline soils.

An annual herb native across parts of southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia, extending to Ukraine and Turkmenistan. It has yellow spring flowers and hairy, spirally coiled fruits armed with thorn-like structures that catch on animal fur and feathers.
A Medicago plant with no stated native origin, it is found throughout the Mediterranean basin. It partners with the nitrogen-fixing bacterium Sinorhizobium meliloti.

Small annual legume native to the Mediterranean region. It is low-growing and clover-like, with rounded three-part leaves often marked by a dark central spot. Yellow flowers appear singly or in small clusters, followed by small spiny pods.
A shrub endemic to eastern Australia, it bears showy red flower spikes through most of the year in ideal conditions. Its woody capsules remain closed until the plant or the fruit-bearing part dies.

Large shrub or small tree endemic to eastern Australia, mainly beside watercourses. It often has drooping branches and bears conspicuous spikes of bright red bottlebrush flowers, especially in spring and summer.

An annual or perennial grass native to southern Africa, Natal grass is introduced and often considered a noxious weed elsewhere. Its open flower clusters carry spikelets densely coated in silky white or pink hairs.

Herbaceous perennial native to much of Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia, usually growing in moist places. It spreads through underground stems, smells distinctly minty throughout, and bears dense rounded clusters of tiny purple flowers. It is used as an edible herb and to make herbal tea.
edibilityNote: Used as an edible herb, like spearmint or peppermint, and to make herbal tea.

summary: Upright perennial herb native to southern and western Europe, including the Mediterranean region. Its wrinkled, softly hairy leaves have a fruity mint flavour and are used in jelly, tea, salads, garnishes and savoury dishes.
edibilityNote: Leaves are used for jelly, flavouring dishes, mint tea, garnishes and salads.

summary: An aquatic flowering plant documented as native in mainland Portugal. There it occurs in mountain lakes and peat bogs, with only four identified locations in central and northern areas. It is assessed as Endangered in mainland Portugal amid continuing declines in its range, habitat and national population.

summary: A creeping perennial probably native to South America and widely naturalized across tropical and warmer temperate regions. Common in grassland, gardens, lawns and moist waterside habitats, it can spread by forming roots where its stems touch the ground.

A small annual native to Europe, upright chickweed has blue-green leaves and delicate white flowers whose green, white-bordered sepals extend beyond the petals. It is a common pasture weed but is not particularly invasive or competitive where introduced.

A rapidly spreading annual plant from tropical America. It forms low circular mats that can climb over nearby plants and has narrow leaves arranged in whorls. Indigenous peoples of Southern Appalachia historically used it as a cooked leafy vegetable.
edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples of Southern Appalachia historically used the plant as a potherb.

summary: A summer-flowering annual native to Turkey, Syria and the Caucasus, it bears spikes of tiny white flowers surrounded by persistent apple-green cups. Its flowering stems are used in fresh or dried arrangements.

Scrambling, semi-deciduous shrub native to New Zealand. Its tough, wiry stems form dense tangled masses or coastal cushions, and its small scented flowers enlarge into translucent fruits with shiny black seeds. Māori, especially children, ate the sweet, juicy flowers.
edibilityNote: The sweet, juicy flowers were eaten by Māori, especially children.

summary: A perennial grass native to the Americas, nimblewill has green or purple stems that bend along the ground as they mature and can root at their lower sections. It forms colonies through seeds and above-ground runners, and its leaves project horizontally.

A flowering herb with a circumboreal distribution across parts of the Northern Hemisphere, bay forget-me-not often grows in moist or wet places and may be aquatic in shallow water. It may be annual, biennial or short-lived perennial, usually flowering from May to September with light-blue flowers that are rarely white or yellow.

An aquatic plant native to wetlands of southern South America, Andean water-milfoil is also used in aquariums. It tolerates very cold water whose surface remains frozen for several winter months, and many waterbirds use it for nest building.

A submerged aquatic perennial native to Europe, Asia and North Africa. Its finely divided leaves grow in whorls, while its small orange-red flowers rise above the water. Broken stem fragments help it spread, and it can form dense invasive mats.

Evergreen shrub or small tree native to southern Europe, North Africa, Western Asia, Macaronesia and the Indian subcontinent. Its leaves contain fragrant oil, while its white or pink-tinged flowers develop into edible blue-black berries that are also macerated in alcohol for Mirto liqueur.
edibilityNote: Ripe blue-black berries are edible and are also macerated in alcohol to make Mirto liqueur.

summary: A submerged annual aquatic plant native to China, the Russian Far East, Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Iran, and parts of Canada and the United States, thread-leaved water-nymph has small, branching stems. Its flowers are either male or female and grow at the bases of branchlets and leaves.

Aquatic annual with an almost worldwide range across temperate and tropical regions; its native origin is not specified. Its narrow leaves have tiny sawlike teeth and midvein prickles, while minute green flowers grow at the leaf bases on separate male and female plants; possibly only female plants occur in the British Isles.

An edible perennial herb native to Europe and Central Asia, where it grows abundantly beside rivers and streams. Watercress is commonly used in salads, though consuming large amounts may irritate the stomach lining and urinary tract.
edibilityNote: Usually used in salads; consuming large amounts may irritate the stomach lining and urinary tract.

summary: Annual flowering plant thought to be native to western South America. Its pale violet, bell-shaped flowers open for only a few hours each day, later developing a deeply lobed, lantern-like covering around the fruit. Introduced widely, it commonly occurs as a weed of cultivated and waste ground.
edibilityNote: Accounts conflict: cooked tender leaves, berries and processed seed jelly are eaten, but the whole plant and berries have also been described as toxic.

summary: Biennial or short-lived perennial native to the Andes of Argentina and Bolivia. It bears strongly night-scented, white tubular flowers above its foliage, and all parts can cause discomfort or irritation if consumed.
edibilityNote: All parts can cause discomfort or irritation if consumed.

summary: A perennial bulbous herb native from southern Mexico to western South America. It bears fragrant, whitish bell-shaped flowers from mid-spring to early summer. Its edible bulb can be used as a garlic substitute or spice.
edibilityNote: The bulb is edible, and the plant is used as a garlic substitute and spice.

summary: Aquatic perennial herb native to the southern United States and Mexico as far south as Michoacán. It has floating or raised yellow flowers and spreads through runners bearing banana-like clusters of leaf buds and thick, starchy roots.

A rooted aquatic perennial native to most of Europe except Ireland and Scandinavia, temperate Asia, and locally Algeria. It has nearly circular floating leaves with wavy edges and clusters of yellow, fringe-edged flowers. Outside its native range, it can form dense mats and is considered a noxious weed in many regions.
edibilityNote: Leaves and flowers are cooked as a potherb; stem interiors are eaten, and seeds are ground for culinary use.

summary: An annual or short-lived perennial herb native to the eastern United States. It forms a hairy rosette of deeply cut or lobed leaves, while its pale-to-deep yellow flowers fade orange, pink or red with age.
A flowering plant native to the Americas, rose evening primrose has small flowers ranging from pink to red. It can spread quickly across yards and fields and may require years of sustained removal.

A flowering plant native to Chile’s Desventuradas Islands and southern Argentina. It has been introduced widely, and both the unimproved plant and its ‘Sulphurea’ cultivar are considered good pollinator plants by the Royal Horticultural Society.

A biennial flowering plant native to Europe and western Asia. It has coarse, deeply lobed spiny leaves covered in white woolly hairs and conspicuous spiny-winged stems, with dark pink to lavender flower heads. Its flower receptacle was formerly eaten like an artichoke, and seed oil has been used for cooking.
edibilityNote: The flower receptacle was eaten historically like an artichoke; seed oil has been used for cooking.

summary: A biennial thistle native to southwestern Europe. Its tall, branching stem and deeply lobed leaves are spiny, while its large flower heads contain many narrow purple flowers and have woolly or cobweb-like coverings.

A prickly pear cactus native to subtropical North America, ranging across the southwestern and south-central United States and northern Mexico. It has yellow flowers, sometimes with red centres, and sweet, spineless purple fruits eaten by humans. The fruits were a reliable summer food for Native American tribes.
edibilityNote: Sweet fruits are eaten by humans and were a reliable summer food for Native American tribes.

summary: A tree-like cactus endemic to mountain habitats in several Mexican states. Its flattened stem joints carry a thin fuzz of white hairs.

A cactus native and endemic to central and northern Mexico, bunny ears cactus forms a dense shrub of flat, pad-like stems. Instead of ordinary spines, it has clusters of tiny barbed hairs that detach at a slight touch and can severely irritate skin; its yellow flowers appear only rarely.
A cactus native and endemic to central and northern Mexico. Its round, flattened blue-grey stem segments carry sharp spines and yellow flowers, followed by fleshy pink or purple fruits.

An annual herb native to mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira. It bears small clusters of yellow flowers and curved fruits divided into several weakly constricted segments, and grows in annual grasslands on siliceous ground.

summary: Flowering legume native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa. It has bird's-foot-shaped pod clusters and produces high-quality forage even in highly acidic, nutrient-poor soils.

A flowering plant native to the former Cape Province and KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, it is also naturalized in Australia. Its flowering stems may reach a foot or more and appear continuously for much of the summer.

A perennial flowering herb native to southern Africa, including South Africa, purple woodsorrel has been introduced on most continents. It grows from bulbs, with three hairy leaflets and solitary white, pink or purple-red flowers.

Bulbous perennial native to the Mediterranean region and Black Sea coasts. It grows on beaches and dunes, often with its leaves and flower stalks largely buried in sand. Its white flowers bloom from August to October and have a subtle scent detectable on still, windless summer nights.
An annual bunchgrass native to most of North America, witch grass has hairy, green to blue- or purple-tinged foliage. Its large, open flower cluster can break off when dry and become a tumbleweed.

An annual grass native to much of the eastern United States and parts of Canada, Panicum dichotomiflorum also occurs in the western United States, where it may be introduced in some climates. Its hairless leaves distinguish it from witchgrass, and it bears a large, open, spreading flower cluster. It grows in sunny, moist habitats and flowers from midsummer through autumn.

Annual flowering grass originally from Central Asia, although some authors place its earliest origins in the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar. It flowers from July to October and grows quickly with little water, making it suited to dry farming.

An annual flowering herb probably native to Macaronesia and the western and central Mediterranean, the opium poppy has grey-green foliage and large red, white or mauve flowers, often dark at the petal bases. Its rounded seed capsules release white latex when wounded, while its seeds and their oil are eaten and contain very low levels of opiates.
edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten whole, milled or roasted; their oil is edible. Seeds contain very low opiate levels, and the oil contains even less.

summary: A flowering plant whose named variety is native to mainland Portugal and Madeira.
Perennial grass native to South America, spreading through underground stems. It often grows in moist, disturbed ground and is a noxious weed where introduced in Hawaii and New Caledonia.

Perennial grass native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas. It spreads through underground and surface-running stems to form thick turf, thriving in salt and brackish marshes and tolerating unusually salty irrigation.

A high-climbing vine native to upland tropical South America, though its exact native range is uncertain because it has long been cultivated there. It has hanging pink flowers and yellow or light-orange fruit containing many seeds in an edible orange aril. Its fruit has been cultivated since pre-Columbian times and remains sold in South American markets.
edibilityNote: Its yellow fruit and orange aril are edible; it has been cultivated since pre-Columbian times and remains sold in South American markets.

summary: A low shrub with no stated native origin, rose-scented geranium occurs in coastal South African fynbos, usually on sandy soil. Its rosy scent comes from essential oil in glandular tissue rather than its nearly scentless flowers, and brushing the hairy stems releases it. It readily colonises disturbed ground and is invasive in coastal southwestern Western Australia.

Evergreen shrub endemic to South Africa. Its cottony-looking leaves stain fingers rusty brown when touched, while its glandular hairs and flowers are typically red, though the flowers are sometimes pink or white.

A scrambling perennial native to the Cape Provinces of South Africa, ivy geranium has somewhat fleshy, circular to heart-shaped leaves with five lobes. Its clusters bear white to mauve flowers, and it can clamber over shrubs on dry, rocky hillsides or coasts.
edibilityNote: The tangy leaves can be eaten as a vegetable.

summary: An upright or scrambling shrub native to the western Cape Provinces of southern Africa, Pelargonium zonale has succulent stems that become woody with age. Its leaves often bear a narrow, dark zigzag band, while its narrow, deep pink petals have reddish lengthwise lines.

Perennial flowering herb native across much of North America, Asia, Europe and parts of Africa. It can grow submerged, floating, on wet mud or in moist meadows, and bears dense clusters of pink flowers. Several Native American groups sometimes used various parts as food.
edibilityNote: Various parts were sometimes eaten by several Native American groups.

summary: Low-growing herb native to China, South Asia and Indochina. Its short-haired leaves are marked with pink or red bands or blotches, and it bears compact flower spikes.

An annual herb native to the United Kingdom and widespread across several temperate regions, water pepper grows in damp ground and shallow water. It has narrow leaves, nodding flower spikes and a pungent taste; wild plants can irritate skin. Cultivated East Asian varieties are eaten, including leaves, young sprouts and seeds.
edibilityNote: In East Asia, cultivated varieties are eaten; Japanese cooks use leaves as a vegetable, young sprouts as garnish, and seeds with wasabi.

summary: A perennial herb widespread across much of North and South America, swamp smartweed grows in saturated or flooded places and is sometimes semi-aquatic. It spreads by underground stems, may root from lower stem joints and bears spikes of small pinkish flowers. It is reported to be edible and, according to at least one author, lacks the pungency of close relatives.
edibilityNote: The plant is reported edible and is said by at least one author to lack the pungency found in close relatives.

summary: A flowering plant whose native range is unclear; as of April 2023, Kew listed it from the Russian Far East through Indochina and Malesia to Australia. It is widely cultivated and naturalized.

Annual herb native to parts of North America and widespread in Canada and the United States. Its upright, ribbed stems carry lance-shaped leaves, sometimes marked by a dark blotch, and small pinkish or greenish flowers.
An annual flowering plant native to Europe. Its linear, stem-clasping leaves grow in opposite pairs, while its small pink flowers form compact heads with usually only one flower visible at a time.
An annual grass native to the Americas, Timothy canarygrass is especially common in Chile and Argentina. It has a narrow cylindrical flower spike with rough-haired, pointed spikelets.

An annual grass native to the Mediterranean region, confused canary-grass grows most actively in spring and autumn. It rests during midsummer heat and short, cool winter days and needs protection from heavy freezes.

Annual grass native to the southern United States, usually found in moist or wet ground and disturbed areas. It has a hairy, roughly oval flower head. Its grains occur at archaeological sites across several states, and it was probably cultivated by pre-Columbian Native Americans.

A flowering grass species recorded in Portugal. Its typical subspecies is native to mainland Portugal and Madeira but introduced in the Azores, while subsp. lusitanica occurs naturally only in mainland Portugal.

A large, solitary palm native to the Canary Islands, it has a broad crown of feather-like leaves and a trunk made distinctive by pruning. Its yellow-orange fruit has edible pulp, although it is not considered a particularly good date. In the Canary Islands, its sap is made into palm syrup, produced only on La Gomera.
edibilityNote: The fruit pulp is edible but considered a poor date; in the Canary Islands, sap is made into syrup, produced only on La Gomera.

summary: A running bamboo native to Fujian and Zhejiang in China, it has closely compressed lower cane sections resembling a tortoise shell. Its canes turn yellow in sun and deepen to gold-orange as they mature; it is considered invasive in several introduced regions.

Perennial flowering herb native to eastern Canada, much of the continental United States and northern Mexico. Its yellow flowers have purple central markings, and each berry sits inside a ten-veined husk. The yellow-green fruit is edible; Puebloan peoples ate it fresh or cooked, while Zuni uses included sauces and dried fruit mixed into bread flour.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten fresh, cooked or dried; Puebloan and Zuni traditions included sauces and bread flour.

summary: A flowering member of the pokeweed family native to Tamaulipas in northeastern Mexico, it has been introduced to California and Portugal.

Evergreen tree native to western North America, chiefly in high-elevation mountains and cool, watered canyons. Its blue-green needles smell pungent when crushed, and wood from slow-grown high-elevation trees is prized for musical-instrument soundboards.

A rare high-elevation pine endemic to California, the foxtail pine has glossy green needles with white inner faces, usually bundled in fives and lasting 10–15 years. Its dark purple cones mature to reddish brown, and Sierra Nevada trees are thought to live up to 3,000 years, though the oldest proven age is 2,110 years.

A deciduous pistachio tree native from North Africa to the Iranian Plateau, it forms a dense crown above a stout trunk with deeply fissured bark. Female trees produce oily pink fruits that ripen to blue, and old trees develop a distinctive grizzled appearance.
edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten as oily nuts; immature fruit may accompany sour milk, resin is chewed as gum, and roots were historically eaten after pickling.

summary: A floating aquatic perennial of uncertain native origin, water lettuce is probably pantropical. Its thick, soft leaves form rosettes above dangling submerged roots, while short runners can link plants into dense mats on ponds and slow-moving rivers.

Large shrub or small tree endemic to New Zealand, originally occurring mainly in the upper North Island. Its leathery dark-green leaves have distinctive fine gray hairs underneath. Fragrant burgundy-red flowers are followed by woody capsules containing sticky, shiny black seeds.

A small evergreen tree endemic to New Zealand, kōhūhū has inconspicuous dark reddish-purple flowers that release a honey-like scent in the evening. Its nearly black ripe capsules split open to reveal black seeds coated in a very sticky substance.
An evergreen shrub native to Japan south of Kanto, China, Taiwan and Korea. It has fragrant white flower clusters, leathery glossy leaves and woody capsules containing black seeds in resinous pulp.
edibilityNote: The fruits are described as not poisonous but not edible.

summary: A flowering plant whose native origin is not supplied; it is introduced in mainland Portugal and the Azores.

An evergreen shrub native to South Africa and Mozambique. Often grown as a climber, it has long thin stems and clusters of pale blue, blue or violet flowers; its sticky sepals sometimes trap animals as large as houseflies.
A perennial grass native to Europe and introduced nearly worldwide. Its stem is distinctly flattened, and it bears a compact, one-sided grey-green flower cluster with purple florets.

A grass native to Mediterranean Europe, North Africa and West Asia, it typically inhabits open, trampled coastal ground but also colonises pavement cracks and gravelly urban sites. Its leaves are strikingly yellow-green, and it occurs as either a small dense tuft or a lanky plant with spreading flower clusters.
Perennial grass native to Europe and Asia. It forms delicate, slightly creeping loose tufts with narrow pointed leaves and a loose, slender flower head, and tolerates shady woodland conditions.

A perennial grass, rough meadow-grass has shiny, tapering leaves with very rough sheaths and short spreading stems. Common in British meadows and pastures, it favours moist, sheltered places and flowers from June through summer.

A low-growing annual herb native to Eurasia, prostrate knotweed forms broad patches of branching stems with tiny green flowers edged in white or pink. It was traditionally used in porridge eaten by Germanic peoples of western Europe.
edibilityNote: Historically used as an ingredient in porridge consumed by Germanic peoples of western Europe.

summary: A deciduous broadleaf tree native to western North America. It releases seed-bearing cottony fluff each spring and has sticky buds with a strong balsam scent. Some Native Americans ate its inner bark and sap.
edibilityNote: Some Native Americans traditionally consumed the inner bark and sap.

summary: Aquatic perennial native to Eurasia, Africa, the Middle East and Australia. Its submerged leaves have conspicuously toothed margins and usually wavy edges, though the waves may be unclear on new growth. It produces overwintering shoots from hardened buds called turions.

An aquatic perennial native to much of the Northern Hemisphere, it generally grows in shallow, clean water. It has narrow submerged leaves and more oval floating leaves, and its great variability and frequent hybridisation can make identification difficult.

summary: Aquatic plant native to quiet or slow-flowing freshwater habitats throughout the Holarctic region, it bears both floating leaves and submerged structures formed from modified leaf stalks. A flexible, discoloured joint just below the top of each long leaf stalk distinguishes it from other pondweeds.

An aquatic herb occurring widely across the Northern Hemisphere, it inhabits standing or slow-flowing fresh water. Its slender stems carry narrow translucent leaves but no floating leaves, and in early autumn the plant breaks apart into numerous overwintering buds.

A flowering plant complex with no native origin stated, it includes hybrids of Potentilla erecta and P. reptans. Its prostrate flowering stems may root at their joints in summer, and it bears yellow flowers.
Evergreen fern native to Europe, Asia and Africa. It has arching divided fronds, each bearing up to five leaflets. A variety with white-striped foliage is widely used to brighten shaded gardens.
A terrestrial fern native to sheltered areas and forests of eastern Australia and New Zealand. It has pale-green, lacy fronds and grows quickly in cultivation, where it can become weedy.
A perennial grass native to Europe. It favors moist, often salty ground such as salted roadsides, and bears hollow stems with spreading flower branches whose lower branches bend backward.

An annual, biennial or perennial herb native to Europe, particularly Spain and Portugal. Its softly hairy growth rises from a spreading root system and bears many yellow flower heads with dense centres and short rectangular outer florets.

Deciduous shrub native from northern Pakistan through northwestern India to China. It is densely branched and very thorny, with white flowers in April and May and orange-red to dark-red berry-like fruits ripening from June to September. Its leaves are used to make herbal tea.
edibilityNote: Leaves are made into herbal tea; berries are eaten with yogurt in a Himalayan therapeutic use.

summary: A shrub native to Taiwan and introduced in several southeastern US states. Habitat loss threatens the species.

A large evergreen oak native to the Mediterranean region. Its mature leaves are dark glossy green above and grey or tawny beneath, while younger growth can be spiny-toothed. Its acorns mature in a single summer.

An aquatic plant native throughout most of Europe and western North America, and also northwest Africa, common water-crowfoot forms mats on the water’s surface. It has thread-like underwater leaves, toothed floating leaves that may be absent in fast-flowing water, and white flowers with yellow centres held above the surface.

Annual flowering plant native to Europe. Once a common arable weed in Britain, it is now rare there and most often occurs in moist places such as spring puddles in meadows. Its mature fruits bear notably spiny seed heads.

Perennial flowering plant native to Western Europe between about 60°N and the northern Mediterranean coast. It has glossy yellow flowers with strongly reflexed sepals and a distinctive swollen underground stem.
edibilityNote: The fresh plant contains a toxin and has caused rare human poisoning; drying removes the toxin, but only animal consumption of dried hay is documented.

summary: Annual herb native to Europe. It has softly hairy stems and tiny yellow flowers borne singly in the leaf axils; some flowers lack petals.

Annual or biennial herb native to Europe. Its erect stem and divided leaves are hairy, while its yellow flowers usually have five petals and five sepals bent backward. It favors moist, disturbed places and is introduced in areas including parts of the United States and Australia.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It occurs in cultivated or abandoned fields, pastures and wasteland, especially on moist, disturbed soils.
Annual herb native to parts of Eurasia and Africa. Rough hairs cover the plant, which bears dark-veined yellow flowers and distinctive knoblike, spherical ribbed fruit.
edibilityNote: Used for food, but the plant part and preparation are not specified.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native across much of North America, from southern Canada to northern Mexico. Its yellow or reddish drooping florets surround a tall central column whose purplish flowers open upward in bands.

Fragrant flowering herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its leaves and flowers have supplied a yellow dye called weld since the first millennium BC, although a related species was used more widely.

A flowering plant native to Europe and Western Asia, weld was once the most widely used source of its namesake natural dye. Its luteolin produces bright yellow, and the plant historically coloured linen, wool and silk, including the Bayeux Tapestry.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in meadows, pastures and uncultivated ground on alkaline soils that are somewhat enriched with nitrogen.

A perennial shrub native to the coasts of Southern California and Baja California, it grows low, sending long reddish stems horizontally. Its dark, glossy leaves have paler, leathery undersides and glands that release sticky, citrus-scented sap. Deep red flower clusters appear from late winter into early spring, followed by small red fruits later in spring.

A shrub or small tree native to the southwestern United States and adjoining northern Mexico, New Mexico locust has bristly shoots, sharp reddish-brown thorns, and showy white or pink flowers. Pueblo Native Americans in New Mexico traditionally ate the flowers uncooked, while some Mescalero and Chiricahua Apache ate the pods raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: Pueblo Native Americans traditionally ate the flowers uncooked; some Mescalero and Chiricahua Apache ate the pods raw or cooked.

summary: A scrambling perennial shrub native to eastern Asia, specifically China, Japan and Korea. Its long arching canes can root at their tips, while fringed stipules at leaf-stalk bases help identify it; in North America it can form extensive, impenetrable invasive stands.
edibilityNote: The hips are used to make tea and have historical and modern medicinal use for constipation.

summary: A dense deciduous shrub native to most of Europe, except the extreme north. Its foliage has a strong apple-like fragrance, while its stems bear many hooked prickles and its pink flowers develop into red hips.
edibilityNote: During World War II, the British relied on its rose hips as presumed sources of vitamins A and C.

summary: An evergreen bramble-forming shrub native to Central and Northern Europe, cutleaf blackberry has deeply divided, jagged leaflets and unusually three-lobed petals. Its blackberry-like fruits have a distinctive fruitier flavour, and wild plants have been grown for fruit since 1770.
edibilityNote: Its blackberry-like fruits have been cultivated since 1770, and commercially important blackberry cultivars were bred from the species.

summary: Bramble shrub native to western and southern Europe and northwestern Africa. Its leaves have three or five leaflets, green above but greenish-white and woolly below, while numerous small prickles arm the plant. Usually pink flowers give way to fruit that ripens dark purple to almost black.
edibilityNote: A spineless form gave rise to cultivars grown for fruit, which is easier to harvest than from wild spiny plants.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to northeastern and northern midwestern North America. It grows in wetlands beside rivers, lakes and swamps, with new leaves that emerge rolled and red to bronzy orange before unfurling.

An annual, biennial or perennial herb native to Europe, marsh dock grows in wetlands such as marshes, moist meadows and shallow stream edges. It has pointed leaves and reddish-brown flower clusters, and its leaf stalks can lengthen when flooded.

A perennial herb native to the Mediterranean. Its divided leaves are joined by bright yellow flowers with rolled, fringed petal edges and pointed, lobed fruit capsules. In Ethiopia, its seeds flavour stews and its leaves season coffee and tea; dried fruit is also sold as a spice.
edibilityNote: In Ethiopia, seeds flavour stews and leaves season coffee and tea; dried fruit is marketed in Western countries as a spice.

summary: A small perennial herb with a circumboreal distribution, alpine pearlwort grows across northern latitudes and in mountain regions farther south. It forms slender or tufted stems and bears solitary white flowers, usually with five petals.

summary: Salt-tolerant perennial native in scattered areas of western Europe, Africa, the Americas and the Caribbean. It is nationally scarce on the southern British and Irish coasts and flowers from July to October.

A perennial, hairy vine native to South America. It has trailing, highly branched, four-cornered zigzag stems, small white or greenish bell- or urn-shaped flowers, and ill-smelling berries that become white or pale yellow when ripe.

A salt-tolerant plant recorded in mainland Portugal that usually grows in coastal or saline places and can be irrigated with salt water. Its ashes were historically an important source of sodium carbonate for making glass and soap.
Evergreen perennial shrub native to Southern California and northern Baja California. It has fragrant, ashy-green leaves and upright whorls of amethyst flowers that open in June and July.

A free-floating aquatic fern native to southeastern Brazil. Its paired broad fronds have bristly, waterproof surfaces, while a third modified frond hangs underwater like a root. In favourable conditions it forms dense invasive mats that can clog waterways and block light from other aquatic plants.

A perennial wetland herb with no stated native origin, it occurs worldwide, especially in shallow brackish, tidal or fresh water. It forms dense stands of narrow upright stems. New shoots and young roots may be eaten raw or cooked, while older roots can be made into flour.
edibilityNote: New shoots and young roots may be eaten raw or cooked; older roots can be made into flour.

summary: A wetland sedge found across Eurasia and South Africa, and introduced to western North America. It spreads through thick underground stems and seeds, producing small brown, bristly fruits in summer. It tolerates salty habitats, although experimentally high salinity noticeably stunted its growth.

summary: Perennial sedge native to Eurasia, parts of Africa, Australia and southern North America. It forms tight clumps with threadlike leaves and small flattened clusters of dark spikelets, typically in moist or alkaline habitats.

A biennial or short-lived perennial flowering plant native to southern and western Europe as far north as northwestern France, it has spiny stems and leaves with bright yellow to orange-yellow flowerheads. Wild-harvested plants are eaten in regional Spanish dishes, while southern Italian leaves are traditionally gathered during Holy Week for an Easter meat pie.
edibilityNote: Young plants, including roots, were eaten raw or stewed in 16th-century Salamanca; wild plants and leaves remain used in regional Spanish and Italian dishes.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. Nettle-leaved figwort grows along scrub edges and roadsides, on rubble, fallow ground and cultivated land, especially in somewhat nutrient-enriched places.

An upright perennial herb native to northern parts of the Northern Hemisphere, marsh skullcap grows beside fens and shorelines. Its blue flowers occur in pairs along one side of the stem rather than at the top.

An evergreen tree native to southern Africa, common in South Africa’s Highveld and Bushveld. It has a graceful, weeping form, dark fissured bark and three-part leaves; historically, its fruits were pounded with water and fermented into beer.
edibilityNote: Historically, the fruits were pounded with water and fermented into beer.

summary: A tufted perennial herb found across northern temperate regions, white stonecrop forms low mats in rocky, freely draining places. Its fleshy, rounded leaves may turn pink under drought stress, while dense clusters of star-shaped white flowers appear in summer.

A small woody succulent shrub native to Mexico, green cockscomb has fleshy lime-green leaves arranged in rosettes. Large clusters of bright yellow, star-like flowers appear from late winter to spring, and the plant tends to become dormant in summer.

An annual herb endemic to the Cape Provinces of South Africa. It has sticky, slightly hairy foliage with deeply divided, toothed leaves, and flower heads combining yellow centers with red-purple rays.
A shrub endemic to Australia, occurring in every mainland state and territory. It has variable paired leaflets, yellow flowers that mostly appear in winter, and long narrow pods.

A hairy, aromatic flowering shrub native to Africa, it has a powerful scent compared variously to mice, wet dog, peanut butter or burnt popcorn. It bears plentiful clusters of bright yellow flowers. The plant is poisonous.
edibilityNote: The plant is described as poisonous; no edible preparation is documented.

summary: An ornamental shrub native to Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, it thrives in wetlands and can form dense thickets. It bears red-orange flowers and persistent pods whose seeds rattle in the wind. The plant and its seeds are poisonous to humans and can cause severe illness or death if eaten.
edibilityNote: Humans who ingest the plant or its seeds may develop vomiting, diarrhea or respiratory failure, and ingestion can be fatal.

summary: An annual flowering grass of unspecified native origin, introduced in mainland Portugal and the Azores. It is naturalized along roadsides and in waste ground and cultivated or uncultivated fields, particularly where the ground is disturbed.

summary: A summer-annual grass native to Asia, giant foxtail emerges from seed in spring and sets seed in late summer or autumn. Introduced to North America, it is a widespread crop weed and a significant pest of maize.

A perennial grass native across much of the Americas, from North America through Central America and the West Indies to South America. It has small knotty underground stems and compact flower heads surrounded by yellow or purple bristles that remain after the seeds fall; it grows in moist and sometimes salty habitats.

An annual grass native to Europe and introduced across most continents, often as a troublesome crop weed. Its flower-head bristles have backward-pointing barbs that hook onto clothing or animal fur. Its seeds are used for beer in South Africa and porridge in Namibia, and have served as famine food in India.
edibilityNote: Seeds are used for beer in South Africa, porridge in Namibia and historically as famine food in India.

summary: An annual grass native to Eurasia, with dense, upright or slightly nodding flower spikes surrounded by stiff bristles. It grows readily on disturbed ground and is the wild ancestor of cultivated foxtail millet.

A perennial or sometimes annual plant native to tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia and parts of the western Pacific, Cuban jute has dark green, diamond-shaped leaves with teeth only on their upper half. Its solitary cream to orange-yellow flowers may have reddish centres, and its ribbed capsules split into segments.

A subshrub or herb native to seasonally dry tropical and subtropical regions spanning Latin America, the Caribbean, Africa, Madagascar, parts of the Middle East and the Indian Subcontinent. It typically grows in disturbed places such as roadsides and pastures.

Herbaceous flowering plant native to most of Europe, Western Asia and northern Africa. It has hairy foliage and clusters of white flowers with deeply notched petals and a distinctive inflated base; occasional pink-flowered plants are usually hybrids with red campion.
An annual herb native to Eurasia. Its stems and opposite leaves are hairy and sticky, and its white-to-pink flowers open at night and release a strong fragrance.
A flowering plant native to Italy, Greece and Turkey. It has been introduced to scattered locations across North and South America, Africa, Europe and Asia.

An annual plant native to North Africa, Europe outside the Arctic regions, and western Asia. Its yellow or occasionally white summer flowers produce seeds used to make mustard condiment and food-grade mustard oil.
edibilityNote: The seeds are used to make mustard condiment and an oil with food applications.

summary: An annual herb native to the western Mediterranean, now established worldwide. It grows on roadsides, wasteland and arable land, bearing pale yellow flowers in late winter and spring. Its young leaves are eaten as salad.
edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten as salad.

summary: Annual flowering herb native to Eurasia and introduced on other continents, where it can be a common roadside weed. It has a tall hairy stem, divided leaves and bright yellow flowers. Its spicy leaves can be used to make wasabi or mixed into salads and other dishes.
edibilityNote: Its spicy leaves can be used to make wasabi or mixed into salads and other dishes.

summary: A perennial wetland wildflower native to Asia and North America, it bears many small white flowers. Its spring and autumn roots are eaten raw or cooked and its leaves are sometimes used as relish, but extreme caution is needed because it resembles poisonous spotted water hemlock.
edibilityNote: Roots are eaten raw or cooked in spring and autumn; leaves are sometimes used as relish. Misidentification with poisonous spotted water hemlock is a danger.

summary: A perennial nightshade native to the Americas, although whether it originated in North or South America is uncertain. Dense, flattened hairs give its leaves and stems a silvery appearance; it also bears variable spines, star-shaped flowers and glossy berries that may persist through winter.
edibilityNote: The whole plant is toxic to humans, even when dried.

summary: A flowering herb or short-lived perennial shrub native to Eurasia, black nightshade bears dull black or purple-black berries in bunches. This helps distinguish it from deadly nightshade, whose berries occur singly; black nightshade also has white rather than purple flowers.
edibilityNote: Only ripe berries and cooked leaves of known edible strains are food; unripe green berries and raw mature leaves can poison, and identification matters.

summary: A prickly nightshade native to parts of South America. Its small ripe fruits are red outside and yellow inside, emerge from spiny green husks, and taste like sour cherries with a hint of tomato.
edibilityNote: The small fruits are edible when ripe, indicated by their easy removal from the stem.

summary: A flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean islands, it has become naturalized elsewhere in the western Mediterranean and Asia Minor. It grows in damp, somewhat shady rocky or disturbed places and is considered invasive in Portugal.

A North American goldenrod, tall goldenrod is native across much of Canada, the United States and northern Mexico. It has finely hairy stems, leaves arranged along the stem and large cone-shaped displays of many small yellow flower heads. It is also naturalized in many other parts of the world.

An annual or perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region of southern Europe, northern Africa and the Middle East. Slender sowthistle has branching stems, deeply divided leaves and heads composed of numerous yellow ray flowers.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, found in South Africa's Western Cape Province. Known as the plain harlequin flower, it has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

summary: Aquatic perennial herb with a circumboreal distribution across northern latitudes. It grows in acidic, nutrient-poor fresh water, producing floating stems with long narrow leaves and separate spherical male and female clusters on the same plant.
