summary: A circumboreal aquatic plant found across North America, Europe, western Asia and Japan. Its thin, grasslike leaves float in shallow calm water, while plants spending longer above water develop shorter, tougher leaves.

A sprawling flowering plant of coastal and inland saline areas, it is an annual or sometimes perennial and tolerates salt. Its small white to pink flowers usually have sepals longer than their petals.

Annual or perennial herb native to Eurasia and the Mediterranean, greater sea-spurrey has narrow stems with fleshy, linear leaves. Its small white or pink-tinged flowers have five petals, while its tiny seeds have winged edges.

A perennial bunchgrass native to temperate and tropical parts of the Americas. Its dense, narrow flower head and upper leaves are sometimes coated with black smut fungus, the source of its common name.

An annual or short-lived herbaceous perennial native to Europe and Asia. Its sprawling stems bear a single line of hairs that changes sides at each node, while deeply divided white petals make each five-petalled flower appear to have ten.

A warm-season grass of unspecified native origin that occurs on both sides of the Atlantic. Its broad, flat, dark-green blades spread by aboveground runners to form a dense, carpetlike layer, making it a popular lawn grass in tropical and subtropical regions.

A medium-sized palm native to South America, the queen palm has feather-like leaves typically bearing around 300 leaflets. Its ripe fruit has sweet, orange, sticky flesh and is sometimes eaten; young buds are eaten as vegetables, pickled or preserved in oil.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruits are sometimes eaten; unexpanded leaves and young buds are consumed, with buds also pickled or preserved in oil.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to much of Canada, the United States and northwestern Mexico. It spreads through underground stems into colonies and bears branching clusters of white, sometimes pink- or purple-tinged flowers whose yellow centres turn purple as they mature.

Rainforest tree native to eastern Australia. It bears clustered white flowers and elongated pink fruit with a refreshing, slightly sour taste; the fruit is eaten fresh or cooked and made into jams and jellies.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten fresh or cooked and used for jams and jellies.

summary: A herbaceous annual or perennial native to Mexico and Central America. Its yellow-to-red flower heads bloom through summer and autumn, and the outer florets have been used in salads and other foods for colour and flavour.
edibilityNote: The outer florets have been used in salads and other foods to add colour and flavour.

summary: A dandelion native to Europe, northern Africa and Asia. It resembles the common dandelion but is distinguished by reddish-brown seed bases and consistently triangular leaf lobes.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. Lesser shepherdscress inhabits annual grasslands, sometimes among rocks, on sandy or stony soils lacking lime.

Annual flowering plant native to Madeira, Morocco and nearly all of Europe. Shepherd's cress grows in meadows, fields and roadsides, typically on human-disturbed soils, though it is locally extinct in Switzerland and Hungary. It has been introduced to the east and west coasts of the United States and southern Chile.

Perennial groundcover native to South America. Its soft, fleshy stems root wherever their nodes touch the ground, while its shiny, dark-green leaves are oval with pointed tips. Small clusters of three-petalled white flowers appear in summer.

Herbaceous plant native to eastern and central North America. Its pale, waxy leaves and stems, sharply angled leaves and tall habit are distinctive; its flowers and shoots can be eaten raw, while the leaves are cooked.
edibilityNote: Flowers and shoots are eaten raw; leaves are eaten cooked.

summary: An annual herb native to areas of Africa and North and South America, desert horse purslane forms fleshy, ground-hugging mats with green to red stems. Its flowers have purple, petal-like sepals, and its curved capsules have two pointed wings. One seed may travel on the detached fruit cap, which floats on water.

Annual clover native to northeast Africa and southwest Asia, with three-part leaves and creamy-white flowers. Most varieties are frost-sensitive, while single-cut and multi-cut groups differ in their regrowth after harvest.

An annual or biennial flowering herb native to Europe, rabbitfoot clover has three slender leaflets and often red-tipped stipules. Its dense, rosy-white flower heads are covered with silky white hairs, giving them their rabbit-foot appearance.
An annual flowering clover native to mainland Portugal and Madeira but introduced in the Azores. It grows in meadows with some soil moisture and is frequent in sown pastures.
Annual clover native to central and southern Europe, the Mediterranean, and southwest Asia as far south as the Punjab. It is grown for fodder and hay, and forms rosettes when grazed or mown.

A flowering plant in the pea family recorded in Portugal. Subsp. brevidens occurs naturally only in mainland Portugal; subsp. striatum is native to mainland Portugal and Madeira but introduced in the Azores.

An annual aquatic herb native from western Canada to Mexico and western and southern South America, it grows in shallow water or beside it. It forms a tuft of narrow, onion-like leaves, with some flowers above water and others in underwater leaf axils.

A perennial flowering plant native to New Zealand, South America, America, Africa, Australia and southern Portugal. Its narrow, linear leaves have memorable parallel lines, and it grows mainly in damp coastal habitats, though it also occurs inland in other wet places.

An annual or short-lived perennial native to Eurasia, scentless mayweed has feathery leaves divided into narrow, thread-like lobes. Its flower heads have white outer florets surrounding yellow centres and appear from June to October.

A Mediterranean annual plant that also occurs very locally in Wales and Ireland. Its yellow, five-petalled flowers usually have a dark red basal spot whose size and colour intensity vary, and the petals fall after only a few hours.

A usually biennial herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, and probably native across much of North America, though details of its range are uncertain. Tower mustard is tall, slim and grey-green, with small creamy flowers, and usually grows in open places on poor chalky or sandy soil.

A deciduous tree with a natural range mainly in southern Europe, extending to Asia Minor and Iran. Field elm is highly variable, often has rough block-patterned bark, and readily sends up new growth from roots and stumps even after Dutch elm disease.
A small to medium-sized tree native to eastern Asia, with small, glossy, toothed leaves. Its bark flakes away to reveal mottled grey, tan and reddish patches, and its winged seeds mature in autumn.

Deciduous tree native across a broad region of central and eastern Asia. It is often bushy, flowers before its leaves emerge, and releases wind-carried seeds. Its unripe seeds have long been eaten in Manchuria, while leaves were eaten raw or cooked with grain, notably during the Great Chinese Famine.
edibilityNote: Unripe seeds were long eaten in Manchuria and became important during the Great Chinese Famine; leaves were eaten raw or cooked with grain.

summary: An aquatic carnivorous plant native to parts of North America, Central America, the Caribbean, the western Mediterranean, southern Africa and southern India. It forms mats of branching, thread-like stems, with tiny bladder traps that draw in and digest prey. Its genome is exceptionally small for a plant.

summary: Small annual terrestrial carnivorous plant native to the Americas, Africa and Australia. It is almost pantropical and is described as the most widely distributed species in its genus. In mainland Portugal it is assessed as regionally extinct, with the last collection dating to 1967 despite later searches.

summary: A shrub or small tree native to Cuba, sweet acacia is evergreen in most places but deciduous in part of its range. Paired thorns grow beside each leaf, and its flowers are used in perfume. Young leaves, flowers and seed pods can be eaten raw or cooked.
edibilityNote: Young leaves, flowers and seed pods are edible raw or cooked.

summary: An annual or herbaceous perennial native to tropical South America, from Colombia and Brazil to Argentina and Chile. It has tall, slender square stems with long gaps between leaves, topped by tight clusters of fragrant lavender to rose-purple flowers from midsummer until the first autumn frost.

A perennial flowering herb native to Canada, the United States, Europe, the Azores and northern Africa. Its creeping stems root at their joints, and plants growing underwater become brownish and look different from those on land. It bears pink flowers with deeper pink lines and heart-shaped seed capsules.

An annual climbing vetch native to Turkey and Malta, and also native in Greece. It has purple-and-white flowers, branched leaf tendrils and hairy seed pods. It is not cultivated for human consumption, and its seeds contain high levels of vicine, which causes favism in susceptible people.
edibilityNote: Not cultivated for human consumption; seeds contain high vicine levels that cause favism in susceptible people.

summary: A slender annual flowering legume native to mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira. It has small bluish flowers and yellow-brown pods usually containing two seeds, occasionally three. It grows in meadows, pastures and cereal fields on siliceous ground.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Perennial flowering herb native to Europe and North America, with smaller native areas in northern Africa and western Asia. It grows in wetlands and along streams, often forming small summer colonies joined by rooting runners. Flowers are usually lilac, pale blue or pale violet, but sometimes nearly white.

A grape native to the United States, sand grape is naturally concentrated in the Ozark Hills of Missouri and Arkansas, with scattered populations farther east and southwest. It is a self-supporting bush of rocky riverbanks and streambanks and has been widely used to breed hybrid grapes and rootstocks.

A climbing flowering vine native to the Mediterranean, Central Europe and southwestern Asia. It attaches to supports with tendrils and bears clustered berries that may be green, red or purple in cultivated plants. Grapes are eaten fresh or dried, their leaves are used in many cuisines, and juice is fermented into wine or vinegar.
edibilityNote: Grapes are eaten fresh or dried; leaves are used in cooking; juice is made into wine and vinegar.

summary: A tall palm native to southern Baja California, Mexico, the Mexican fan palm is also found in Sonora. It is highly variable and now occurs in many regions around the world.

A perennial flowering herb native to South Africa's Cape Provinces, bulbil bugle-lily produces showy spikes of orange, reddish or purplish flowers. It often spreads through small cormlets formed along the flowering stem, sometimes creating dense colonies.

A tiny aquatic flowering plant native to Europe, Africa and parts of Asia, rootless duckweed is described as Earth’s smallest vascular plant. Its rootless, rounded green body floats on quiet water and buds into new plants. Long used as inexpensive food in Myanmar, Laos and Thailand, it is rich in protein and starch.
edibilityNote: Long used as inexpensive food in Myanmar, Laos and Thailand; its green part is protein-rich and its dormant turions are starch-rich.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An aquatic plant of fresh and brackish water, recognisable by long, thread-like leaves that give it a stringy appearance. It has long, tendril-like roots and distinctive horn-shaped seeds.

A plant native to Asia, Russia, Ukraine and Romania, Syrian bean-caper has thin stems with sparse, fleshy, waxy leaflets. Its long taproot can produce new plants from fragments, and it forms colonies in dry, gravelly, salty or disturbed places.

A medium-sized tree whose native origin is not stated, found across Africa from Senegal to northern South Africa. It bears large hanging clusters of brown, sausage-shaped fruit and foul-smelling, bell-shaped flowers that open at night and are pollinated by bats. Its fibrous fruit contents are often considered inedible, but are locally eaten cooked; the Maasai also ferment the pulp into strong beer.
edibilityNote: Fibrous fruit contents are often considered inedible but locally eaten cooked; Maasai ferment the fruit pulp to make strong beer.

summary: A deciduous tree native to mainland Africa, the African baobab has an exceptionally broad trunk that may comprise several stems fused around a hollow core. It can remain leafless for about eight months in the dry season, while its large white hanging flowers stay open and fertile for only one night.
edibilityNote: Traditionally eaten in Africa: roots and fruit are edible; dry fruit pulp is soaked for juice, and young leaves are cooked.

summary: A succulent shrub or tree of unspecified native origin, found in southern Africa. Its upward-curving, usually unbranched branches have four to six angles and strong constrictions that divide them into inverted-cone-shaped sections; the winged edges bear teeth and spines.

sources.title: Euphorbia cooperi N.E.Br. ex A.Berger
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering succulent perennial endemic to southeastern Southern Africa, including South Africa, Malawi, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. It forms large, sprawling clusters with spiny-edged leaf rosettes at branch tips and produces vivid red-orange flowers, often blooming in winter.
A free-floating flowering plant native to Europe and Asia. It has circular floating leaves and small white flowers, and can form dense invasive mats in North American waterways.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Hydrocharis morsus-ranae
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to the southeastern United States, it has sword-like blue-green leaves edged with distinctive white threads and masses of hanging cream flowers in early summer. Its fruit can be cooked and eaten after the seeds are removed, while the large petals are eaten in salads.
edibilityNote: Fruits are cooked after seed removal; large flower petals are eaten in salads.

summary: A bulbous orchid native to the Mediterranean Basin, the giant orchid flowers from January to April. Its bulb is edible when cooked.
edibilityNote: The bulb is edible when cooked.

summary: An orchid of unspecified native origin, found across Europe, the Mediterranean and the Near East to Iran. Its dense flower spike bears a violet-brown hood, an unspotted purplish-green three-lobed lip and a downward-pointing spur. It grows in meadows and scrub clearings, often on somewhat moist clay or stony soils.

summary: Annual succulent herb whose native origin is not stated. It has simple, broad leaves and a self-supporting growth form.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to the southern and eastern United States. It often has several stems and produces clusters of dark-red tubular flowers in spring, followed by smooth light-brown fruit; its seeds are poisonous.
edibilityNote: The fruits contain poisonous saponins, and the seeds are poisonous to humans.

summary: A perennial herb native to the eastern and central United States, violet woodsorrel grows from an underground bulb and has three heart-shaped leaflets and lavender-to-white spring flowers. All parts are edible and used in salads, but only moderate amounts are advised because its oxalic acid can be poisonous in large quantities.
edibilityNote: Flowers, leaves, stems and bulbs are edible and traditionally eaten, including in salads, but large quantities may be poisonous because of oxalic acid.

summary: Perennial ornamental plant native to the United States, Canada and northeastern Mexico. Its hairy, grass-like leaves surround shorter stems bearing yellow, star-shaped flowers, which open in the morning and usually wilt in hot afternoon sun; despite its appearance, it is not a grass.

A small palm native to the southeastern and south-central United States and northeastern Mexico, the dwarf palmetto grows in habitats ranging from swamps and floodplains to occasionally drier sites. Its rounded fans of leaves and unusual cold tolerance among North American palms make it distinctive, and older plants can become tree-like.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean from western Morocco and Portugal to Greece and western and southeastern Turkey, it bears reddish-purple spring flowers and red-to-black fruit. In Cyprus the fruit is baked into village bread, in Crete it flavours pomace brandy, and in the Northern Sporades the shoots are eaten as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: Fruit is baked into bread, used to flavour pomace brandy, or roasted for a coffee-like drink; shoots are eaten as a vegetable.

summary: A non-photosynthetic orchid native to Europe and Russia, with sporadic presence in North Africa and parts of the Middle East. Usually beige-brown rather than green, it blends into woodland leaf litter and obtains its nutrition through soil fungi linked to tree roots.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Neottia nidus-avis
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A carnivorous plant native to the New World, the yellow pitcher plant ranges from southern Alabama through Florida and Georgia to the coastal plains of Virginia and the Carolinas. Its vibrant yellow rolled leaves form pitchers whose slippery surfaces, downward-pointing hairs and digestive fluid trap insects.
An annual flowering plant occurring in southern Europe. It has hairy stems and leaves, a stiff-haired capsule, and red flowers marked at the base with a black spot edged in yellow.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Glaucium corniculatum
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

summary: A deciduous flowering tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar. It has rounded, two-lobed leaves and conspicuous fragrant pink flowers, followed by long seed pods. Young leaves and flowers are edible; in Philippine cuisine, the citrusy, sour leaves flavor soups or are prepared as a pickle condiment, while flowers are used in pickles and curries.
edibilityNote: Young leaves and flowers are edible; leaves flavor Philippine soups or pickles, and flowers are used in pickles and curries.

summary: This herbaceous perennial orchid has no stated native origin; it is widespread in mountainous regions across much of Europe and is also found in Algeria, Morocco and western Siberia. Its leaves carry dark oval spots, while dense flower spikes range from pale pink to purple or white with darker streaks.
A shade-loving fern native to central and southern China, Korea, Japan, the Ryukyus, Taiwan and Vietnam. It commonly grows on old walls and has been introduced to many other parts of the world.

An aromatic deciduous shrub native to cool temperate Eurasia and North America, often forming dense colonies from root suckers. Its spring catkins usually occur as male and female flowers on separate plants, though plants may change sex between years. Dried leaves and fruits have seasoned food and beer, and leaves make tea; people who are or may be pregnant should not consume it.
edibilityNote: Dried leaves and fruits are used as spice or beer flavouring, and dried leaves as tea; avoid during possible pregnancy.

summary: A large, clump-forming herbaceous perennial native to the coastal Serra do Mar Mountains of southern Brazil. Its enormous leaves have spikes underneath and along their stalks, while tiny red-green flowers form conical branched clusters. Many European cultivated and feral plants labelled as this species are actually the hybrid Gunnera × cryptica.

Deciduous fern native to Europe, North Africa and West Asia, growing in woodland bogs and beside streams. Its stout underground stems can eventually form a woody, trunk-like base, while brown spore-bearing tips make some fronds resemble flowers.
edibilityNote: In some places, young shoots called fiddleheads are eaten and said to taste like asparagus; the source marks this claim citation needed.

summary: A tall wetland perennial native to Kazakhstan's Irtysh River valley, sweet flag has iris-like leaves with crimped edges and a fragrant smell when crushed. Young inner stems are eaten raw, while peeled roots have been boiled and simmered in syrup for candy; however, ingestion may be toxic, and food use is banned in the United States.
edibilityNote: Young inner stems are eaten raw; peeled roots are boiled in syrup for candy. US food use is banned because ingestion may be toxic.

summary: A tussock-forming, grass-like evergreen perennial native to Europe, the Atlas Mountains, Turkey, Iran and Central Asia. It has bright-gold foliage with green edges and grows in wetlands such as marshes, fens and shallow-water margins.

A tall perennial of wetlands and river margins, forming colonies with hairy, often three-lobed leaves. Its large flowers range from white through pink to deep red, usually with a dark maroon centre, and attract bees.
edibilityNote: Leaf buds, young leaves, flowers, seeds and roots are documented as edible; immature seed pods can be prepared like okra.

summary: A large deciduous shrub native to temperate eastern Asia, including China, Mongolia, southeastern Siberia, Korea and, rarely, central and northern Honshū in Japan. Its paired flowers change from white to yellow or pale orange, and children sometimes suck their sweet nectar, but its red to black berries are mildly poisonous and should not be eaten.
edibilityNote: Children sometimes suck sweet nectar from the flowers; the berries are mildly poisonous to humans and should not be eaten.

summary: Clubmoss with a pan-tropical distribution and possible native status in the Azores. It favors bogs and is described as the largest clubmoss, with long rhizomes and tall leafy uprights.

summary: A flowering plant native throughout eastern and central North America, late figwort grows in dry woods. Its rounded flowers are deep reddish-purple inside, greenish to brown outside, and resemble a horse’s mouth with an overbite; hummingbirds commonly visit them in late summer.

Herbaceous perennial native to the Balkans through Greece, Crete and the Aegean Islands, and southwestern Anatolia. Its large purple floral structure smells like rotting meat and attracts fly pollinators, while its broad divided leaves may have cream-flecked veins.

A perennial flowering plant native to the western and central Alps, rare in much of its Swiss, Austrian and Italian range but commoner in the French Maritime Alps. Its nodding light-blue to blue-purple flowers have straight or slightly curved nectar spurs, unlike the hooked spurs often seen on hybrids sold under this name.

An evergreen succulent perennial native to southeastern Europe and Asia Minor. Its sprawling stems carry fleshy blue-green leaves, while inconspicuous spring flowers are surrounded by bright yellow bracts. Ingestion causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and its milky sap can severely irritate skin and eyes.
edibilityNote: Ingestion causes nausea, vomiting and diarrhea; the milky sap can also severely irritate skin and eyes.

summary: Fern native to eastern North America and across Eurasia. It grows in wet habitats such as swamps, bogs, marshes and streambanks, with fertile fronds bearing spore clusters underneath.

An aquatic fern native across parts of Europe and Asia, from central and southern Europe to Vietnam. Its four-part leaves resemble four-leaf clover and may float in deep water or stand upright in shallow water or on land. In mainland Portugal it underwent severe decline during the last century and was assessed as Critically Endangered.
edibilityNote: The plant has reportedly been used as food in some places for more than 3,000 years.

summary: Evergreen fern native to the Balearics, Corsica, Crete, Sardinia and Scilly, with a wider range across Europe, Asia and North Africa. Pale reddish-brown scales cover the frond undersides, which become visible when the leaves roll up in summer. It can withstand drying and recover when rewetted.

A fern found mainly around the Mediterranean Basin and eastern Atlantic, with isolated records as far north as Ireland and Poland. It is difficult to distinguish from black spleenwort; leaflet shape is unreliable, while spore size viewed under a microscope is more consistent.
A deciduous tree or densely branched shrub native to the Mediterranean region. Its small, glossy, three-lobed leaves have smooth edges and fall unusually late in autumn.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin, mastic has a strong resinous smell and leathery, deep-green leaves. Its aromatic resin is harvested as a spice and chewing gum, while its tart, raisin-like fruit is edible but not commonly eaten.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible but uncommon as food; the aromatic resin is used as a spice, flavouring and chewing gum.

summary: A flowering plant endemic to the Mediterranean region, shrubby hare's-ear is an evergreen shrub of sunny hills, walls and rocky places. It has simple blue-green leaves and clusters of tiny yellow flowers that bloom from June to September.

A perennial coastal flowering plant found across much of Europe, Macaronesia, parts of West Asia and North Africa. Its woody-based stems and divided leaves are fleshy; fresh leaves are eaten in salads, while stems and leaves are cooked and several parts are pickled.
edibilityNote: Fresh leaves are eaten in salads; stems and leaves are cooked, and stems, leaves and young seed pods are pickled in several European traditions.

summary: A flowering plant with two listed subspecies native to mainland Portugal, though native status is not stated for the species as a whole. It has rigid, lance-shaped leaves, with blunt basal leaves and pointed stem leaves. In Portugal it grows in open scrub, clearings and perennial grassland on stony or rocky, usually limestone-derived soils.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it inhabits dry meadows and scrub clearings. It is often associated with very short-lived water runoff channels over stony ground derived from marl, schist or greywacke.

A perennial herb of unstated native origin, Oenanthe globulosa grows in temporarily flooded depressions with muddy, clay-rich soils. In mainland Portugal, a 2020 assessment knew only a few populations concentrated around Sintra and classified it as Vulnerable amid continuing habitat decline.

summary: A flowering perennial native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, hemlock water-dropwort grows in damp grassland, wet woodland and along waterways. It has hollow, grooved stems, fleshy tubers that release yellowish oily fluid when cut, and leaves that smell deceptively like parsley or celery. All parts are extremely toxic.
edibilityNote: All parts are extremely toxic; roots mistaken for parsnips have caused severe and sometimes fatal human poisoning.

summary: A tall perennial herb of the Mediterranean coast, it occurs from Spain and Morocco to Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Cyprus and Turkey. It has alternate leaves and yellow, unisexual flowers in rounded clusters, and grows in scrubland and rocky areas.

An evergreen flowering subshrub native to Western Europe, including the Iberian and Italian peninsulas, France and Sardinia, intermediate periwinkle forms broad mats. Its whitish-blue flowers bloom from late winter to early spring.

A perennial plant native to central and southern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, the southern daisy has creeping underground stems. Its apparent flower is actually a cluster of many tiny flowers, with white outer florets surrounding yellow tubular ones.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it grows in dry scrub and along the edges of evergreen thickets and woodland, particularly on limestone or marl soils.

sources.title: Staehelina dubia L.
sources.attribution: Info Flora, plazi (2021). Info Flora Schweiz - Asteraceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/qmbbhk accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant in the daisy family, Pulicaria odora grows in pine woods, bushy places and sandy ground. Its leaves are cooked and may then be edible.
edibilityNote: The leaves may be edible after cooking.

summary: A plant with no native origin stated in the supplied information, Mediterranean phagnalon can grow up to 50 centimetres high.
Shrub native to Mediterranean-basin countries in Europe, North Africa and Western Asia, as well as Iran, Iraq, the Arabian Peninsula and the Canary Islands. It has simple broad leaves and dry fruit.

A compact evergreen shrub native to southwestern Europe. It has narrow, aromatic green leaves and tight yellow flower heads in summer. The leaves are used in Mediterranean dishes and cocktails for an olive-like flavour.
edibilityNote: The leaves add an olive-like flavour to Mediterranean dishes and cocktails.

summary: An annual or perennial shrub depending on locale, Helichrysum stoechas grows in dry, rocky and sandy places; its native origin is not stated. It has greyish-green leaves and small, round yellow flowers that may appear in spring or in July and August. Its leaves and flowers have an intense fragrance used in perfumery and aromatherapy.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, it favours dry roadsides, waste ground, uncultivated land and clearings in degraded scrub, especially on basic soils.
An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it grows in dry pastures, meadows and uncultivated ground.

sources.title: Echinops strigosus L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A wild thistle native to Portugal, Spain, Morocco, Algeria and Gran Canaria. It is used locally to curdle milk in traditional sheep's and goat's cheesemaking.
edibilityNote: Used locally as a coagulant in artisanal sheep's and goat's cheesemaking.

summary: A highly branching perennial of unstated native origin, it is common throughout the Mediterranean Basin. Its narrow toothed leaves are sticky, hairy and unpleasant-smelling, while a single plant can carry many yellow flower heads.

An annual flowering plant found across the Mediterranean Basin and western Europe, although its native range is not explicitly identified. It has white petals around a yellow-orange centre and blooms during rainy seasons. Its whole flowers are crushed for essential oil, whose composition varies with where it grows.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it commonly occupies disturbed farmland, waste ground and roadsides. A black border extending to the base of its floral bracts may help identify it, but this feature still requires confirmation.

sources.title: Centaurea pullata L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Low-growing annual herb native to the Mediterranean region. It has orange-yellow flowers from April to June and colonizes dry coastal areas.
A herb with subspecies recorded from southern Europe, North Africa, the Canary Islands, Madeira and Turkey. It has broad leaves and usually yellow or orange, many-petalled flowers.

An evergreen perennial native to the Mediterranean region, with aromatic silvery-white leaves and sprays of yellow, daisy-like flowers. In Maghrebi mint tea, it is used during winter as a bitter substitute for or supplement to spearmint.
edibilityNote: Used in Maghrebi mint tea during winter as a bitter substitute for or supplement to spearmint.

summary: An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it grows in degraded scrub, dry meadows, roadsides and uncultivated ground, with a preference for clay soils.
A hardy perennial flowering plant native to southern Europe and Morocco. It has narrow, serrated leaves and clusters of small flowers.
edibilityNote: Leaves may be chopped and eaten raw as a herb or added to soups and stews.

summary: A flowering plant with documented native origins at subspecies level: subsp. microcarpa is endemic to mainland Portugal, while subsp. procumbens is endemic to the Iberian Peninsula.
A hardy flowering perennial native to Portugal, Morocco, Algeria and Libya. It forms a sprawling mass of red flowers throughout summer and readily self-seeds.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira but introduced in the Azores, it grows in annual grassland, scrub clearings, roadsides, uncultivated ground, rocky outcrops and walls.

sources.title: Campanula erinus L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial herb distributed around the Mediterranean, though the source does not state a native origin. Its above-ground parts range from sparsely hairy to grey-felted or glandular-hairy, and its stems may become woody at the base. From April to July it bears wavy petals that may be violet, rust-coloured or yellowish.

sources.title: Matthiola fruticulosa (L.) Maire
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A flowering plant native to Portugal and Spain, the Lusitanian bellflower is the namesake of a group of closely related species.

A biennial herb found across western Asia, northern Africa and most of Europe, rampion has light blue or violet bell-shaped flowers and a thick, turnip-like root. It was once widely grown in Europe for leaves eaten like spinach and an edible root used like a radish.
edibilityNote: Historically in Europe, its leaves were eaten like spinach and its parsnip-like root like a radish; the thick root is explicitly edible.

summary: A climbing flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region of southern Europe and northern Africa. It can grow to 2.5 metres or more and is sometimes cultivated as a garden plant beyond its native range.

An evergreen shrub, rarely a small tree, native to Mediterranean Europe and North Africa. Its white or pale pink flowers emerge from reddish-pink buds in winter, followed by dark blue-black fruit with an unusual metallic blue colour.
An annual flowering herb native to mainland Portugal. It grows in clearings of dry scrub on stabilized dunes with acidic, sandy soil.

An annual flowering herb distributed around the Mediterranean, the Canary Islands and southwest Asia. Its hairy, branching stems bear deeply divided, vivid pink or white petals, and it grows on sandy beaches and cultivated land.

sources.title: Silene colorata Poir.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A fodder shrub widespread through the Mediterranean Basin, North and East Africa, and the Arabian Peninsula, Mediterranean saltbush has small gray leaves. Its leaves are edible, and the plant tolerates severe drought and highly alkaline or saline soils.
edibilityNote: The leaves are edible and were reportedly gathered and eaten by poor returnees from Babylonian exile around 352 BCE.

summary: A shrub native to south-western Europe and western North Africa. It has wavy grey-green, hairy leaves and pink-to-purple flowers with five petals.
A flowering shrub native to southwestern Europe and western North Africa, grey-leaved cistus bears pink to purple flowers. Dense short hairs give its three-veined leaves a greyish-white appearance.

A low-growing flowering plant whose two recorded mainland Portuguese subspecies are native there. The typical subspecies favours rocky or sandy ground, especially limestone, while the other occurs in low-scrub clearings on coastal cliffs.

A shrubby flowering plant native to Europe and Africa, silver broom occurs across the western and central Mediterranean, including parts of southern Europe, the Balkans and northwestern Africa. It has also been introduced to Germany.

A medicinal flowering plant native to Europe, northern Africa and Western Asia. It bears spherical flower heads, usually with yellow petals, though var. coccinea has red petals, and favors dry grassland and rocky, lime-rich ground.

A bush native to the western Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Maghreb, Erica umbellata has clusters of three to six flowers at the tips of its stems. Its flowers are intensely pink or purple, but occasionally white.

An evergreen flowering shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin and parts of East Africa. It has needle-like leaves and many small, honey-scented white flowers, while its exceptionally hard, heat-resistant wood is used for smoking pipes.

An evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Mediterranean Basin and Western Europe. Its rough red berries are edible and sweet when reddish, and they ripen in autumn alongside the next crop of white, bell-shaped flowers.
edibilityNote: Red berries are edible and sweet when reddish; eaten fresh but more often made into jam, marmalade, yogurt, brandy and other alcoholic drinks.

summary: A climbing herb native across southern and central Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia, it has anticlockwise-twining stems, heart-shaped leaves and bright red berries. Most of the plant, including its tuber, is poisonous, but young shoots are reportedly harvested while their saponin content is low and eaten as a vegetable.
edibilityNote: Most parts, including tubers, are poisonous; young shoots are reportedly harvested while saponin is low and eaten as a vegetable.

summary: A low-growing flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It inhabits dry, sunny and usually rocky low scrub, particularly on limestone-derived ground.

sources.title: Fumana thymifolia (L.) Spach ex Webb
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Pine native to the Mediterranean region, with an outlying population in the eastern Mediterranean. It has paired, slender yellowish-green needles and narrow cones that mature glossy red-brown, then open gradually over several years or faster when exposed to heat.
edibilityNote: Its pine nuts are used in Tunisian and Maltese desserts, while its resin flavours Greek retsina wine.

summary: A pine native to southern Atlantic Europe and parts of the western Mediterranean, maritime pine has the longest and most robust needles among European pines. Its large cones open slowly over several years or after heating by a forest fire, releasing winged seeds.

Evergreen shrub endemic to Portugal. It forms compact, densely branched cushions with a bright green exterior, dry brown stems and sharp spines, and often grows on limestone near the central-west coast.
A gorse native to France, the Iberian Peninsula and parts of the Maghreb.
A flowering perennial occurring in southern temperate Europe and Siberia; it is not native to Ireland. It forms an upright bush with wiry, usually spiny stems and deep pink-and-white flowers.

A small flowering tree or shrub native to the Iberian Peninsula and northwestern Africa. Its young branches have silky silver hairs, and yellow flowers appear from April to July; it thrives on dry, poor and rocky ground.

A perennial flowering plant native to parts of Africa, Europe and Asia, it scrambles over nearby vegetation using tendrils. It has winged, floppy stems, pairs of narrow leaflets, pinkish-red flowers and seed-filled pods.
A flowering legume native to the Mediterranean. Its seeds are cultivated on Santorini and cooked into fava santorinis, a purée typically served with onion, olive oil and lemon juice.
edibilityNote: The cooked seeds are made into the Greek purée fava santorinis.

summary: A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal, it was described in a 1913 account as a low, hairy annual of dry hills in Estremadura, coastal Alentejo and the Algarve. That account noted purplish flowers in dense heads and pods covered with bristle-bearing scales.

Perennial flowering legume native to the southeastern United States, especially sunny, dry habitats. Its wiry, hairy stems bear leaves of three leaflets and yellow-orange flowers during summer and fall.

Leguminous tree native to East Africa, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and southern Africa. Its long, woody seed capsules contain bright red and black seeds, which are used decoratively and as fish poison.

An aquatic perennial native from East Asia through northern Indochina to central and northern India, with isolated Caspian locations. Its flowers can regulate their temperature, and seeds have germinated after about 1,300 years. Rhizomes and seeds are widely eaten; petals, leaves and rhizomes should be cooked because eating them raw risks parasite transmission.
edibilityNote: All parts are edible; petals, leaves and rhizomes are recommended cooked because raw consumption risks parasite transmission.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It grows in exposed herbaceous clearings among scrub and oak woodland, sometimes on banks, with a preference for limestone soils.

sources.title: Valeriana tuberosa L.
sources.attribution: Info Flora, plazi (2021). Info Flora Schweiz - Caprifoliaceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/udbe2g accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Poisonous evergreen shrub native to the northern and western Mediterranean region. It has dense, narrow dark-green leaves, fragrant white flowers and red autumn fruits; all parts are considered highly poisonous if consumed.
edibilityNote: All parts are considered highly poisonous when consumed.

summary: A perennial herb native to Israel, with a wider Irano-Turanian and Mediterranean distribution. It is covered in star-shaped hairs that feel unpleasant, and a touched or damaged flower abruptly sheds its entire corolla after about 30 seconds.

An annual flowering herb native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It grows on roadsides, fallow or cultivated ground, open land and banks, favouring disturbed, somewhat nutrient-rich soil with some moisture.

A herbaceous perennial with no native origin specified, wild madder has woody, square climbing stems and glossy evergreen leaves arranged in whorls. Its small, pale green-yellow flowers appear from April to June, followed by fleshy berries that turn black when ripe.

A low-growing flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It has an unmistakably strong smell and grows in sunny, dry, rocky open scrub on sand, limestone or shale; contact may cause skin inflammation triggered by light.

summary: A woody-based perennial herb native to mainland Portugal. Its foliage is pale blue-green to grey, and its dense flower clusters have yellow to greenish petals; contact may cause skin inflammation triggered by light.

sources.attribution: F. Munoz Garmendia, C. Navarro, A. Quintanar, A. Buira, S. Castroviejo, plazi (2015). Flora Iberica / Vol. IX: Rhamnaceae - Polygalaceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/3xha5s accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: A perennial flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It usually bears one or two large, bright-yellow flowers and grows around woodland edges, oak woods and scrub, generally in shaded, somewhat moist places.

sources.attribution: F. Munoz Garmendia, C. Navarro, S. Castroviejo, plazi (1999). Flora Iberica / Vol. VI: Rosaceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/7jx4n7 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An evergreen shrub from Mediterranean-climate scrub between Gran Canaria, Morocco and Portugal and the Levant, Mediterranean buckthorn has glossy, leathery leaves and small, fragrant yellow-green flowers. Its red-brown fruits darken to black when ripe.
Flowering plant native to mainland Portugal. It occurs in dry, usually stony soils, especially limestone, in scrub clearings, dry grassland and banks.

Flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean region, including mainland Portugal. Populations may have yellow or white flowers, and in Portugal it occurs in scrub clearings and woodland edges, particularly from the central coast and west to the southern Algarve.
A perennial grass native to Europe, Africa, western Asia and the Arabian Peninsula. It is self-supporting, with simple broad leaves and dry fruit.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and belonging to the plantain family.

Terrestrial orchid native around the Mediterranean and Middle East, from Morocco and Portugal to Hungary and Iran. It grows from underground tubers and flowers between March and June in its native habitats. Its brown, velvety lip has three rolled lobes and a complex blue-to-violet marking.
An annual herb of unstated native origin, with a self-supporting form and simple, broad leaves. Its flowers are visited by several insects, including brown argus butterflies.
Evergreen shrub native to the western and central Mediterranean. It has narrow, leathery dark-green leaves and scented creamy-white flowers, followed by purplish-black berries.
Annual flowering herb native to northern Africa south to Tanzania, southern Europe and southwestern Asia. It is locally naturalised elsewhere, including Great Britain.

A terrestrial orchid occurring throughout the Mediterranean, it has a glossy, iridescent purple-blue patch surrounded by reddish-brown velvety hairs. Its flowers are pollinated exclusively by the wasp Dasyscolia ciliata.
Tree native to the Mediterranean Basin, from Morocco and Portugal east to the Levant. It is commonly known as the green olive tree or mock privet.
Deciduous tree native to Central and Southern Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia. Its pale brown buds distinguish it from the black-budded common ash, while its leaflets are notably slender.
A flowering plant native to the western Mediterranean. Among mallows in its genus, it is unique for the two-lobed structure just beneath each flower.
A perennial herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, West Asia and Macaronesia. It is a small, self-supporting plant with simple broad leaves and an association with freshwater habitats.
Small, self-supporting annual herb native to southern Europe, western Asia, North Africa, the Horn of Africa and some oceanic islands, including Madeira, the Canary Islands and Socotra.
Annual flowering herb native to mainland Portugal. It has narrow, hairy leaves and yellow petals marked with purple veins, and grows in dry grassland and stony or sandy ground.

sources.title: Linum setaceum Brot.
sources.attribution: F. Munoz Garmendia, C. Navarro, A. Quintanar, A. Buira, S. Castroviejo, plazi (2015). Flora Iberica / Vol. IX: Rhamnaceae - Polygalaceae. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/3xha5s accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: An erect subshrub endemic to Portugal, particularly the southwest. Its graceful, four-sided stems bear cream or white flowers with purple stamens, and it inhabits sandy acidic soils, especially stabilized dunes.

An edible wild garlic native to the Mediterranean and nearby areas from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey and Palestine, rosy garlic has loose, fragrant pinkish-to-lilac flowers. Its bulb has a powerful smell and flavour.
edibilityNote: Documented as edible; the bulb is specifically described as having a powerful smell and flavour.

summary: A flowering plant with a mainland-Portuguese endemic subspecies and an Iberian-endemic subspecies. The mainland-Portuguese subspecies is legally protected, while the Iberian-endemic subspecies is not.
A perennial herb endemic to the central Iberian Peninsula in Spain and Portugal, it has white flowers. Oil from the flowers is used in some pain-relieving lotions.

Perennial evergreen flowering vine found across parts of Africa, Mediterranean Europe and Asia. It has flexible thorny stems, leathery heart-shaped leaves with spiny edges, fragrant yellowish or greenish flowers, and berries that turn from red to black but are unpalatable to humans.
edibilityNote: The berries are described as insipid and unpalatable to humans, but not explicitly inedible.

summary: An evergreen shrub native to Eurasia and parts of northern Africa, butcher's-broom has flat, stiff shoots that resemble spine-tipped leaves. Small greenish flowers appear singly at their centres in spring, followed on female plants by red berries.
edibilityNote: The berries caused reported poisonings, mostly in children, including 107 cases in 1995–2007 and four acute cases in Lombardy in 2010–2011.

summary: A bulb-forming herbaceous perennial found in the Mediterranean Basin, Armenia and northwestern Iran. It produces a pyramidal cluster of star-shaped, milky-white flowers, each marked by a pale green central vein. It grows in fields, dry grassland, waste ground and rocky terrain.

A perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region of southern Europe, northern Africa and the Middle East. Its highly branched stem and small fruits help distinguish it from similar asphodels, while its numerous white flowers have a central brown streak.
Flowering plant native to the western and central Mediterranean. It occurs in coastal scrub and disturbed places; in Portugal it also occupies open dry thickets, hedges and abandoned dry orchards.

sources.title: Asparagus albus L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

summary: Flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. In Portugal it grows in low dry scrub, open evergreen woodland and stony banks, usually on limestone.
A flowering herb native to the Iberian Peninsula and northern Morocco. It has thin leaves and white flowers, and wild plants in Spain and Portugal are gathered for use fresh or dried as a food herb.
edibilityNote: Wild plants are collected in Spain and Portugal and used fresh or dried as a food herb.

summary: An annual herb, Italian woundwort has a self-supporting growth form, and its flowers are visited by the Green-striped White butterfly.

A small plant, sometimes a shrub, native to southern Mediterranean regions including Iberia, Sicily, northwestern Africa and the Canary Islands. It has grey woolly stems, fernlike silver-green leaves and dark blue or violet flowers held above the foliage; its aromatic leaves smell more like oregano than other lavenders.
A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and present in mainland Portugal.

A tall perennial herb native to the British Isles, Mediterranean Southern Europe, North Africa, the Near East and the Caucasus. It has hairy stems and soft purple-to-violet summer flowers. This aromatic sage flavours food and tea, and its flowers can be added to salads.
edibilityNote: Used as a food flavouring and tea; flowers can be added to salads.

summary: Flowering plant found in the western Mediterranean; its native origin is not stated. In Portugal it occupies seasonally waterlogged but unflooded ground that dries in summer, often on clay derived from limestone.

summary: Perennial herb found mainly around the Mediterranean, from Macaronesia to southwestern Turkey; its native origin is not stated. Its heart-shaped leaves clasp the stem and bear translucent and black dots, while the fruit capsules have prominent glands.

summary: Evergreen oak shrub or tree native to the Mediterranean region and North African Maghreb, from Portugal and Morocco east to Cyprus, Anatolia and the Levant. It is usually a low shrub and historically hosted kermes scale insects used to make crimson dye.

A spreading shrub oak native to Portugal, western Andalusia and rarely Galicia in Spain, and Morocco. It usually lies low and spreads by runners. Its insect-induced galls are harvested commercially for dyeing.

An evergreen oak native to the western Mediterranean, with most of its population in the Iberian Peninsula and smaller populations in Northwest Africa. It has a dense, rounded crown and small, leathery leaves. Humans have eaten its acorns since Neolithic times, including toasted and ground as flour for soups or breads in southern Iberia.
edibilityNote: Acorns are eaten; in Neolithic southern Iberia they were gently toasted, ground into flour, and used in soups or breads.

summary: Annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira. It grows in Mediterranean scrub clearings, dry orchards, hedges and roadsides, generally on alkaline clay.

An annual flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, Scorpiurus vermiculatus occurs in fields, fallow ground and grassland. A 1913 description records hairy upright or rising stems and thick pods coiled in one plane, with stalked, broadened warts covering their backs.
A herbaceous flowering perennial found across most of southern and central Europe and North Africa. It has broad simple leaves, square stems and small two-lipped flowers in loose clusters.

A shrub of the Mediterranean region, found in southern Europe and northern Africa, Mediterranean buckthorn has a tangled, many-branched form with thorn-tipped young stems. Its inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in winter, and its yellowish fruits ripen black.
edibilityNote: The berries are very bitter and purgative, and are toxic to humans in large quantities.

summary: An annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin. Its variable leaves and flowers accompany red blooms, usually appearing from December to May.
edibilityNote: The plant is edible, but its acid-lemon-flavoured leaves contain high oxalic acid levels that may be dangerous in large amounts.

summary: A deciduous or semi-evergreen oak native to the western Mediterranean region of the Iberian Peninsula, the Portuguese oak can live for up to 600 years. Its leaves usually fall in mid-to-late winter, while its oblong acorns mature within six months.
A low-growing woody flowering plant native to Spain and mainland Portugal. It favours scrubland and flowers from November to May.
Perennial herb of broadly Mediterranean or southern European origin. The entire plant is grey and woolly, with opposite, toothed leaves and pinkish wine-coloured flowers.

summary: Flowering plant whose subspecies Nepeta tuberosa subsp. tuberosa is native to mainland Portugal. It belongs to the mint family.

A bushy evergreen shrub native to Iberia, Morocco and western Turkey. Its narrow aromatic grey-green leaves contrast with dense heads of small dark-purple flowers, topped by large purple bracts resembling butterfly petals.
A flowering plant whose subspecies Erophaca baetica subsp. baetica is native to mainland Portugal.

A flowering tree or shrub native to China and Japan, Japanese camellia grows naturally in forests. Its leathery dark-green leaves accompany rose or white wild flowers, while thousands of ornamental cultivars offer many flower colours and forms. Its processed leaves can be made into aromatic tea and contain caffeine and catechins.
edibilityNote: Processed leaves are used to make aromatic tea and contain caffeine and catechins.

summary: Evergreen shrub native to the Appalachians of eastern North America, from Alabama to coastal Nova Scotia. It keeps waxy, deep-green leaves for up to eight years and bears showy white, pink or pale-purple flowers, mainly in June. In the southern Appalachians it often dominates the forest understory, forming dense thickets called “laurel slicks” or “laurel hells.”
edibilityNote: Leaves may be poisonous, but no human food use or ingestion context is given.

summary: Herbaceous perennial native to the Mediterranean region, although its exact natural range is uncertain after 2,000 years of cultivation. Its fringed flowers have a spicy, clove-like fragrance; wild flowers are bright pinkish-purple, while cultivars come in many colours.
edibilityNote: Its fragrance was historically used in vinegar, beer, wine, sauces and salads.

summary: A large deciduous shrub or small tree native to the southern Balkan Peninsula, common lilac bears dense clusters of sweet-smelling flowers, usually lilac to mauve but occasionally white. Its flowers are edible and used to flavour honey, sugar, food and other sweets.
edibilityNote: The flowers are used to flavour honey, sugar, food and other sweets.

summary: A large evergreen flowering tree native to the southeastern United States coastal plain, from Virginia to central Florida and west to eastern Texas. It has stiff, dark-green leaves and large, waxy white flowers with a strong lemon-citronella fragrance.

A herbaceous perennial native across much of western, southern and central Europe, the Caucasus and eastward to central Asia, alpine forget-me-not has a highly restricted British presence. There it occurs at two sites: limestone grassland in the North Pennines and high ground around Ben Lawers.

A perennial orchid native to southwestern Eurasia, from western Europe through the Mediterranean to Iran. Its compact flower head has a distinctive pyramidal shape, with pink to purple, rarely white, flowers and a scent described as foxy.
A small palm native to North America. Its extracts are used medicinally, including traditional use for urinary and prostate conditions.

An agave found only in the Chihuahuan Desert, lechuguilla often spreads through underground offshoots into large colonies. It flowers once, then dies, and has tough, rigid leaves tipped with points sharp enough to penetrate clothing or leather.
edibilityNote: In Mexico, salt- and mineral-rich water stored in flowering stalks is sold as a sports drink.

summary: A palm native to the Philippines, the areca palm grows straight with numerous crowded leaflets. Its nuts are chewed with slaked lime and betel leaves for stimulant and narcotic effects, but they are addictive and linked directly to oral cancers.

A deciduous flowering shrub native to woodlands of the southeastern United States, oakleaf hydrangea has large lobed leaves with silvery-white undersides that turn red, bronze and purple in autumn. Its upright, cone-shaped flower clusters open white and age to pink or brown, depending on the cultivar or seedling.

A critically endangered conifer native to southern Brazil and also naturally found in northeastern Argentina, Paraguay and northern Uruguay. It has thick, triangular leaves with razor-sharp edges, and large cones containing many edible, nut-like seeds that are extensively harvested in southern Brazil.
edibilityNote: The seeds are edible, widely harvested in southern Brazil and eaten as a winter snack, including boiled.

summary: An Australian rainforest tree naturally distributed from northeastern New South Wales to tropical Queensland. Its bright red flowers form circular, wheel-like clusters, while its boat-shaped fruits hold many thin seeds.

Perennial herb native to eastern Australia, with long, strap-like leaves arising from underground stems. Its leaf tip has three prominent points, with the side points as long as or longer than the middle one. Seeds may be ground into flour, while the flowers and leaf bases are also edible.
edibilityNote: Seeds may be ground into flour for Indigenous Australian damper; flowers and leaf bases are also eaten, with leaf bases chewed for water.

summary: A woody climber native to Australia, Malesia and the southwestern Pacific region. Its juvenile and mature leaves differ, and it bears white or cream tubular flowers with purple markings followed by capsules containing winged seeds.

Fruit tree native to the eastern and central United States. Its deeply plated bark is distinctive, and its orange fruit is astringent when unripe but sweet when ripe; ripe fruit may be eaten raw, usually after softening, or cooked or dried.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten raw, usually after softening, or cooked, dried, fermented or made into desserts, jam, molasses and candy.

summary: Deciduous tree native to China, the Japanese persimmon has broad, stiff leaves and sweet, slightly tangy fruit. Astringent varieties are edible only when soft-ripe, while non-astringent varieties such as ‘Fuyu’ can be eaten firm.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten ripe or dried; astringent varieties require soft ripening, while non-astringent varieties may be eaten firm.

summary: A rock-growing orchid endemic to eastern Australia. It usually grows on rocks, sometimes forming large colonies, and bears spikes of usually pink flowers from late winter to spring, though timing varies with climate.

A large plant widespread in eastern Australia, the Queensland grasstree can develop a tall, many-branched trunk and grey or bluish-green leaves. Ngunnawal people make a sweet drink by soaking its flower spike and eat the growing leaf-stem portion and white leaf bases.
edibilityNote: Ngunnawal people soak the flower spike for a sweet drink and eat the growing leaf-stem portion and white leaf bases.

summary: Shrub or tree endemic to eastern Australia, including Lord Howe Island. It has thin bark, usually white flowers borne singly on short side shoots, and fruit that can remain on the plant for a few years.

Palm tree endemic to the east coast of Queensland and New South Wales, Australia. Its single trunk has a swollen, regularly scarred base, while its long fronds often twist so their outer leaflets stand nearly vertical. Ripe fruits are bright red and contain one seed.

A large shrub or small tree native to the eastern coast of tropical South America, extending south to Uruguay and parts of Paraguay and Argentina. Its ribbed fruit changes from green through orange and scarlet to maroon; the edible fruit ranges from tart to sweet with cultivar and ripeness and is used mainly in jams and jellies.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten and used in jams and jellies; taste varies from tart to sweet with cultivar and ripeness.

summary: A shrub native to eastern Asia—northeastern China, Japan, Korea and southeastern Siberia—the rugosa rose naturally grows along sandy coasts. It forms dense, prickly thickets and has deeply wrinkled leaves with scented flowers ranging from dark pink to white. Its hips are edible raw or prepared as jam, syrup or tea.
edibilityNote: The hips can be eaten raw or made into jams, syrups or tea.

summary: A deciduous succulent endemic to southern Madagascar, it grows as a spiny shrub or tree with thick, water-storing stems. Its leaves fall during the long dry season, and young plants begin as tangled stems before developing a strong central trunk.

A perennial herbaceous orchid widespread across central and southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Its flower has a hairy, variably patterned petal resembling a bee’s abdomen; northern populations are almost exclusively self-pollinating, while a solitary bee pollinates it in the Mediterranean region.
edibilityNote: Root tubers were ground into salep in the Ottoman Empire; salep remains used in traditional dishes in Turkey and across the Middle East.

summary: A liverwort, it was typically absent from urban sites in one tropical Ecuador study despite occurring at a nearby pristine site. The study suggested sensitivity to human effects such as wastewater and heavy-metal pollution.

A sprawling annual weed whose native origin is not stated, red nightshade occurs in Europe, western Asia and northern Africa and is naturalized in Australia and North America. It is hairy, with white or purple-tinged flowers followed by dull red or orange-yellow berries, depending on the subspecies.

A medium-sized deciduous tree native across Europe and temperate Asia and to northern Morocco, silver birch is mainly mountainous in the southern parts of its range. It has white, peeling bark and slender, often drooping twigs, while its roughly triangular leaves turn yellow in autumn.
edibilityNote: In spring, tapped sap may be drunk fresh, concentrated like maple syrup, or fermented into wine.

summary: A flowering bromeliad indigenous to warmer parts of the Americas, from the southern United States to northern Argentina and Chile. It forms rounded clumps on trees, fences and wires, using hosts mainly for support rather than nourishment.
edibilityNote: The Pima of Mexico occasionally eat its flowers for their high sugar content.

summary: An Arctic–alpine fern native to Europe and parts of Asia. It produces separate sterile and fertile fronds and colonises acidic rocky slopes, often where snow remains late in the year.

summary: An evergreen trailing rock-rose native to most of Europe. Its bright yellow, saucer-shaped flowers have touch-sensitive orange stamens, while garden varieties range from white to deep red. Individual blooms are short-lived, but flowers appear in abundance through summer.
Annual flowering herb native to Great Britain, Iceland, central Europe and Western Asia. It blooms in July and August and is a known host of flax rust.

A perennial flowering herb whose native origin is not specified, wild basil has square, upright, hairy stems and pink, violet or purple two-lipped flowers. Its leaves are used to flavour food and make herbal tea.
edibilityNote: The leaves are used as an aromatic herb in food dishes and to make herbal tea.

summary: A deciduous tree endemic to woodlands of the southeastern and south-central United States, winged elm grows slowly and tolerates many soils. Broad, thin corky wings develop along older branchlets, and the leaves turn bright yellow in autumn.

A large deciduous tree native to the Balkans, horse-chestnut has fallen-leaf scars shaped like horseshoes with seven “nails.” Its spring flowers are usually white with yellow-to-pink markings, followed by green spiky fruits containing glossy brown conkers.
edibilityNote: Raw seeds, leaves, bark and flowers are toxic and should not be eaten; young, fresh seeds can cause sickness.

summary: A deciduous shrub native to the Americas east of the Rocky Mountains and south to Bolivia. It bears large clusters of white summer flowers and drooping clusters of dark purple-black fruit; only ripe berries cooked with their seeds removed are suitable for food.
edibilityNote: Only ripe berries should be cooked and have their seeds removed; traditional jams, jellies and syrups use cooked, strained fruit.

summary: A herbaceous perennial of unstated native origin, lady's bedstraw is widespread across most of Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia. In medieval Europe its dried plants stuffed mattresses and its flowers were used in cheese making; in Denmark, it is traditionally infused into spirits.
edibilityNote: In Denmark it is traditionally infused into spirits; its flowers were used in medieval European cheese making.

summary: Annual herb of unstated native origin, found on Mediterranean scrubland hills and beneath stonework or concrete structures. It has alternate leaves that may be divided two or more times.

Annual flowering plant native to North Africa, Europe, and parts of western and central Asia as far as the western Himalayas. Its pear-shaped fruits carry a small, toothed crown formed by the remains of the flower.

A perennial flowering herb native to Europe and Asia, greater knapweed bears purple, thistle-like flower heads crowned by ragged purple-pink outer parts. Its deeply divided leaves form a clump at the base, and its flowers attract bees and many butterflies.

A perennial flowering herb native across temperate Eurasia from Britain to Japan. Its violet-blue or purplish-blue bell-shaped flowers grow in tight clusters and bloom from June to September. Garden varieties also include white, pink and blue forms.

Epiphytic fern native to tropical southeastern Asia, eastern Australia, Hawaii, Polynesia, Christmas Island, India and eastern Africa. Its large, banana-like fronds form a nest that collects water and decaying plant matter. Sprouts are eaten in Taiwan, while young fronds are eaten in Polynesia, often cooked with coconut cream.
edibilityNote: Sprouts are stir-fried or boiled in Taiwan; young fronds are eaten in Polynesia, often cooked with coconut cream.

summary: A slow-growing tree fern native to Hawaii, hāpu‘u pulu produces fiddleheads that supply pulu, a material used as mulch or padding. Women also used pulu as a menstrual absorbent.

A tropical flowering tree native to tropical Asia and Australia. It has glossy leaves, bright pink or red flower clusters and bell-shaped fruit that ripens red, pink or white-streaked. The ripe fruit is eaten raw despite its bland flavor; flowers are eaten in Indonesian salads, and the skin is cooked into syrup in Guyana.
edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten raw; Indonesians eat the flowers in salads, and in Guyana the fruit skin is cooked into syrup.

summary: A flowering plant native to south Texas, Mexico, Belize, Venezuela and the Caribbean. It bears yellow flower heads throughout the year and commonly grows as a weed in lawns, roadsides and paths.

A tall perennial flowering plant native to North Africa, most of Europe and parts of Asia. Its robust stems and narrow leaves are densely hairy, while the large purple-pink flowers have four notched petals.

An evergreen shrub native to Mexico and naturalized in Florida. Its white flowers emerge from chains of red or salmon-pink bracts resembling shrimps, and its long blooming periods attract hummingbirds and butterflies.

A perennial yam vine native to Africa, Asia and northern Australia, air potato forms bulbils on its stems and potato-like tubers underground. Its twining stems always twist counterclockwise around supports.
edibilityNote: Some varieties have edible tubers; boiling removes their bitterness. Tiwi people ritually cook and eat the tubers during the kulama ceremony.

summary: A low, spreading deciduous shrub native to central and eastern Canada and the north-central and eastern United States, lowbush blueberry has glossy blue-green leaves that turn red in autumn. Its white or pink bell-shaped flowers produce small, sweet, dark blue to black berries.
edibilityNote: Wild blueberries are used in Maine’s state dessert, blueberry pie.

summary: A biennial flowering plant native to central and eastern North America. It has square, narrowly winged stems and fragrant pink, occasionally white, flowers with yellow markings that form a central star.

Perennial sunflower native to North America, including south-central Canada, the eastern and central United States, and northeastern Mexico. Its stems and leaves have stiff hairs, and it spreads through underground rhizomes in sunny open forests and forest edges.

An evergreen shrub native to southern Argentina and Chile and symbolic of Patagonia. It has shiny, box-like leaves, arching thorny branches and blue-black berries eaten fresh or made into jam and alcoholic drinks.
edibilityNote: The blue-black berries are eaten fresh, made into jam and added to alcoholic drinks such as calafate beer.

summary: A flowering plant primarily native from eastern Siberia to Korea and northern and central Japan.

A woodsorrel that likely originated in North America and is now found worldwide. Its clover-like leaves have three leaflets, and its small flowers have five yellow petals; it is often considered a weed.

An evergreen tree native to the Brazilian states of Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Goiás and São Paulo. Its round, purplish-black fruit grows directly on the trunk and contains sweet white or pink flesh; it is eaten raw or made into preserves, juice and alcoholic drinks.
edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw or made into jellies, jams, juice, wine, tarts and liqueurs; it has been cultivated in Brazil since pre-Columbian times.

summary: A deciduous tree native to the Appalachian, Ozark and Ouachita mountain regions of the eastern United States. Its large leaves cluster at branch tips like umbrellas, while its large, unpleasant-smelling spring flowers develop into red, cone-shaped fruits.

A shrub or occasional small tree native to eastern North America, eastern Mexico, the Bahamas and Cuba, groundsel tree often grows in salty or brackish wetlands. Female plants develop conspicuous snowy-white, cotton-like flower heads in autumn. Its seeds are toxic to humans.
edibilityNote: The seeds are toxic to humans.

summary: An evergreen shrub or tree originating in Southeast Asia, rose-apple has glossy mature leaves and white or greenish-white flowers with many long stamens. Its ripe fruit has a strong floral scent, crisp watery flesh and usually one or two loose seeds; it is eaten raw, cooked in regional recipes or served with spiced sugar in Southeast Asia.
edibilityNote: The ripe fruit is eaten raw or cooked in regional recipes and is often served with spiced sugar in Southeast Asia.

summary: Non-stinging nettle-family plant that grows on walls and rubbish. Its pollen can cause allergies.
edibilityNote: It was once used to make certain metheglins.

summary: A very small fern native to Europe, East Asia and eastern North America. It grows exclusively on limestone and other calcium-rich rocks, with bluish-green, heavily divided fronds.

Herbaceous perennial native to Europe, from Spain north to Belgium and Poland and east to Ukraine. It has slender green to grey-green leaves and tight clusters of usually dark pink to purple flowers, which are occasionally white.

A creeping aloe native to South Africa’s Western Cape and adjacent parts of the Northern and Eastern Cape. It sprawls over rocky ground, while its leaf-bearing tips often turn upright; drought can redden and curl its fleshy leaves inward. Unlike most aloes, it flowers in summer.

Lily native across Eurasia, from Portugal through Europe and Asia to Mongolia. Its scented, backward-curving flowers are usually spotted pink-purple but can range from nearly white to nearly black, with numerous blooms on vigorous plants.
